utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Good morning, Mr. Harland.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, good morning.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that in your report and in your interest overall the enclaves occupied quite a big space; am I right? They occupied quite a big space in your interest well, as well as in our overall crisis, I would say; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce 1D982. 1D982. 09639 is the Prosecution document number. 09639 is the Prosecution number before 1D928.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me jog your memory. We had a very unusual crisis regarding Gorazde, which entered many books and memoirs of its participants. In Pale -- the Prosecution number is 09639. And that's -- that's not it. This one can be removed from the screen. In Pale, there were Mr. Akashi, Mr. Stoltenberg, Mr. Churkin. Mladic was somewhere around Gorazde. General Rose was in the centre. Do you remember where radio ham operators were who reported back from Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there were some radio operators reporting back from Gorazde, but I can't remember any of the details about it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But they were in Sarajevo. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We will see a document later to show how the American experts showed interest in that endeavour. We still don't have the document. 09639 is the Prosecution document number. 09639. This is a United Nations document, and that event speaks about the 16th of -- yes, that's the document. Can we go straight to page 2. First of all, are you familiar with this document, sir?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Page 2, please. And while this is happening -- no. It has happened. What I'm saying is this: Muslim lines collapsed intentionally in order to pull in the Serb forces and possibly NATO and the United Nations. And let me describe the situation for you. Near Gorazde a number of military observers found themselves on their lines without informing the Serb sides. When the Muslims withdrew, they remained in the Serbian encirclement and that was clarified over the radio. Let's look at page 2 and let's see where it says Gorazde crisis, and I continue reading in English because there is no Serbian -- no, there is Serbian: "The Eastern Bosnian enclave Gorazde has collapsed. The lines have been broken. One monitor of the United Nations was killed and the other was wounded. The credibility of the United Nations in the country has been reduced. In other parts of Bosnia, the Serbian forces hold about 150 members of the United Nations. Commander Rose made three requests for close-air support, in English, for close-air support." [In English] "These were rejected by special representative of Secretary-General Akashi, who was in Pale negotiating with the Serb leadership when the big Serb advance occurred." [Interpretation] Do you agree that this was not so much a big advance on our part as it was the process of their withdrawal and pulling our forces in towards our lines? Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was certainly the -- the view of General Rose that the sudden collapse and withdrawal of the Bosnian forces could not easily be explained simply by the presence of the Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then paragraph 3 where it says Gorazde crisis. Towards the bottom where it starts "Gorazde --" [In English] "Following a second use of the NATO airpower on Monday, [Interpretation] And then it says at 11 --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Given that nobody is looking at the B/C/S version, why don't we zoom in the English version for the benefit of the witness so that it be clearly be -- we can collapse this. Yes. Let's continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then the last paragraph on the screen: "[In English] At 11.45 a demonstration of close-air support was made, and at 12.25, General Mladic was verbally warned that air support [sic] would be used if the shelling did not stop immediately." And then the last sentence in the same: [In English] At 14.19, following further low passes by NATO aircraft, two US F-18 jets struck at a tank and two armoured personnel carriers." [Interpretation] And can we now -- "[In English] At 14.33 General Mladic was warned again, but at 15.08 a tank opened fire again on Gorazde. Flares were dropped, a final warning was delivered to General Mladic 14 -- 15.45, and after some time, a fax was received from General Mladic assuring UNPROFOR that an order had been passed to cease fire." [Interpretation] Do you agree with me that that operation by the Serbian Army around Gorazde was a counter-offensive -- or, rather, that it was a response to the previously launched offensive from the enclave of Gorazde?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That -- that was not our understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I must admit that it was our own fault, because we were not very good at propaganda. So we did not present the situation very well, although there is proof that we did process, saying that we were being attacked from the enclave of Gorazde? Thank you. And now let's go to page 4. Page 4 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Mr. Harland, do you wish to comment on what Mr. Karadzic said in response to your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Propaganda thing.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at some level it was true. The Serbs were very bad at putting out their side of the message even when they -- even when they had points that they needed to justify. They -- for example, they never allowed us -- I think Dr. Karadzic's daughter, we used to have this debate with her. They never allowed us internationals free access to territories controlled, or let alone for journalists controlled by Republika Srpska, and that naturally created a suspicion among us and among journalists that they had a lot to hide. When they would say we have sniper victims in Grbavica or the Bosniaks are making an offensive out of Gorazde, we would say, Let us see. But very often, they did not give us permission, whereas the other side, who they always accused of perfidy and lying, generally gave us rather open access to the whole battle-field, but it's a big subject.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. As you saw, Mr. Karadzic, put your question to the witness instead of making submissions yourself. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, do you agree with me that at first when you were still not there the journalists did have open access and that we suffered so much damage from some of the journalists that that -- those damages were even bigger than the damages from shelling? Do you remember the scandal around Trnopolje when a team of journalists fabricated a whole picture and thus put us in a very dire position?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time I was there access to the Serb areas was very restricted, but I must admit it was something of a vicious circle. You didn't give access, and so the general -- the journalists became suspicious and hostile, so you didn't give access. There was a very negative relationship between Republika Srpska and the Western press.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry that you were not there from the very beginning. You would have seen what the journalists did to us, but we will have documents to prove that. But what I'm saying here is this: I'm sure that you know that Muslims launched a number of offensives and were never shelled, and whenever we launched a counter-offensive we always had to suffer consequences. We were always shelled. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that we in the international community never used force against the Bosniak side, but we often did against the Serbs and occasionally against the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On that same page, which is page 4 -- we don't have page 4. There is a comment on your behalf. I'm going to read it in English. Before that it says the ban on contact -- [In English] "The ban on contacts with the UN was lifted when Akashi and a senior international delegation was received in Pale yesterday. The Serbs indicated that the door was still open for an agreement for the cessation of hostilities throughout B and H." [Interpretation] Do you agree with me that we advocated a forced cease-fire in the entire area, not only in some areas until a political agreement could be reached, whereas at the same time the Muslim side advocated a partial and temporarily limited cease-fire; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you agree with me that our explanation for that was that during those cease-fires they were consolidating their ranks and preparing for further fighting? That was our explanation for their request. Do you agree that our explanation was well grounded, that it was justified?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was certainly one of the reasons, and they would be quite clear with us about that, that they wanted to buy time because they needed weapons or time for training, yes. But there were also -- there was a bigger reason, in our view, and that was that if there was a general cease-fire, a really good general cease-fire across Bosnia and Herzegovina, they would be left with the relatively small territory they held, and they fear that if it was a really good cease-fire that over time those boundaries would become fixed and they would be left on a very small part of the territory. So for both reasons that you -- or for the first reason you mentioned, the need to buy time to re-arm but also the need to keep the situation open, they had very little interest in an effective general cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you that we always claimed that there would be no fait accompli and that the final solution would be reached at the conference. In that sense, I'm afraid, and we have proof to that effect, that they wanted an entire Bosnia, that nothing short of that would have done. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were on the Bosnian government side also very sharply divided. Different members would give us different opinions. Some had very maximalist goals and believing that one day the Bosniaks would control the entire country if they could just buy enough time. Others felt they should take an agreement that was on offer, and they, in fact, regretted that they had not accepted earlier agreements like Cutileiro or Owen-Stoltenberg or HMS Invincible agreements. I think they were a little divided. And sometimes changed their own minds, sometimes would have one position and then the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember that you were there in 1995, and that was described by Ambassadors Bildt and Holbrooke. Do you remember that when a decision was reached to put a stop to the war they asked the Muslims, What do you want us to do on your behalf? How should we -- how should we negotiate, for you to have 30 per cent of power and 50 per cent of Bosnia, or do you have to have 100 per cent and 30 per cent of Bosnia? Do you remember that? And they openly told them, You can't have 100 per cent of power and 100 per cent of Bosnia. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present when that was said, but I've heard it quoted before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now pay attention to your comment which I'm going to read in English. [In English] "It appears that Serbian President Milosevic is attempting to appeal to the best interests of the Bosnian Serbs: Pointing out that a major conflict with NATO is in nobody's interests except Sarajevo's. Pale, however, appears defiant and ready to take the risk that NATO will not intervene to defend the designated ... areas. "The Bosnian government reaction to the collapse of Gorazde has been strong. "Prime Minister Silajdzic has attacked the UN for failing to execute its mandate to deter attacks on the safe areas, including Gorazde. In a statement last night he said that the UNPROFOR had betrayed Bosnia. He condemned the UN for proposing to demilitarise Gorazde in return for a promise from the Serbs not to attack it." [Interpretation] And then on the following page, again part of your comment: "[In English] The Bosnian government has long seen UNPROFOR's presence here as a substitute for lifting the arms embargo." [Interpretation] Looking at your comments can we say that they confirm that the Muslims wanted to use you on their side during the war?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at page 7, please, in the same document. Can we look at the comment again, which is a bit lower. The second sentence: "[In English] By appearing to support hardline Presidency member Ganic in his visit to Bihac, UNPROFOR lost credibility with Abdic's people in the northern pocket." [Interpretation] Does it arise from this that UNPROFOR was not on the entire Muslim side but on the side of some Muslims, not on the side of Abdic's Muslims but rather on the side of Izetbegovic's Muslims? Your comment here is very insightful, I would say.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say I can't remember what I wrote the comment about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, let me give you the context. Ganic, who was a hard-liner in the Presidency, had gone to Bihac to counter Abdic who was also a Muslim and two-third or, rather, three-fourths of that province were in favour of Abdic, but Abdic was a pro-European Muslim. You're saying that maybe that should not have been done because UNPROFOR lost credibility with Abdic's Muslims by supporting Izetbegovic's or Ganic's Muslims when they made the visit to the 5th Corps possible. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually have to admit I can't remember the specific context, but I can confirm that this is a document I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 8 there is Eastern Bosnia, and here are our remarks, and a general comment, and I'm going to read in English. "[In English] Srebrenica, long quiet, is more active than in recent months. "Serb commanders appear to be intent to [sic] stopping the north-south flow of traffic between Srebrenica and Zepa ..." [Interpretation] The following paragraph: "[In English] There are reports of persistent provocations of Dutch units in Srebrenica. The identity of the provocateurs is not shown, though UNMOs suspect that BH soldiers are involved." [Interpretation] You say that for a long time Srebrenica was quiet, and then Serb commanders decided to interrupt the communication between Srebrenica and Zepa when they realised that weapons were being procured from there, and they also realised that UN troops had been provoked by Muslim soldiers, at least according to UN observers; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now let's go back to Gorazde again. Muslims played a trick. They led UNPROFOR members very far to their lines. Then they withdrew very quickly and left them in our encirclement, and we were not aware of that. Their lines collapsed, and their trick was a success; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not on the field at Gorazde. I was at the other end of the radio with General Rose when the -- the two or was it the four of his observers, his British observers that he called the joint JCOs, were exposed by the Bosnian -- by the Bosnian withdrawal, and he certainly shared your assessment that the withdrawal had been not forced by Serb military pressure and that it may even have been the intent of that withdrawal to expose his observers, one of whom I think died of his wounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the transcript doesn't say that the -- the trick worked because ultimately we were bombed by NATO. That should be reflected in the transcript. 1D982. Could we have that, please. General Janvier to the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Would you like to tender that previous report?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, certainly. However, I would just like Mr. Harland to confirm that that was when we were bombed, on that occasion. That's what the document says, a tank was hit, two armoured vehicles, I think an ambulance was hit, too, and then General Rose kept that photograph in his office and it said, "Bravo NATO." Remember, an ambulance had been hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly remember the -- a photo and General Rose's commentary. The -- if I remember correctly, the close-air support attacks that were made against the three Serb vehicles was -- was because they had refused to comply with a demand from General Rose to cease-firing, I think. It was not immediately related to the incident that you were describing, which is the actual moment of the Bosnian withdrawal that left the -- left the four -- the two or four British observers exposed. But I must admit I can't remember exactly the sequence, but I -- that's how I think it was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, the 16th of April report will be admitted as --

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: And just to note, Your Honour, that report is one of the associated documents referred to in Mr. Harland's statement from paragraphs 104 to 108 mentioned in our original notification of 29 April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Would you like it to be admitted as part of Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will Exhibit P829.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 1D982 is what we have now, although that's the old number. I mean, 204 is the old number. 1D982 is the number, actually. So now I'd like us to have 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 -- page 6. General Janvier's report. It's the penultimate paragraph. I'll read it out in English, "Similar": "[In English] Similar to what happened in Gorazde (spring 94) the BiH can attempt to draw UNPROFOR including the rapid reaction forces or NATO into the conflict on the BiH side. Sudden abandoning of positions along the confrontation line, the simulation of a collapse of the enclave or alarming reports from Bosnian side on the situation in the enclaves will be indicators for this. A stronger involvement of the international community could be interpreted by the Bosnian Serb army as an incentive to step up operations and try to eliminate the enclave, as well as retaliate against UN forces." [Interpretation] Do you agree with this conclusion made by General Janvier? I understand that you're not a military expert, but this is a general question, after all.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can confirm that that was the view of both General Rose and General Janvier. I had my -- I had my doubts, I have to say, but I'm not a soldiers, not a military expert.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This was sent on the 10th of July, 1995. The document was -- that's right. It is the 10th of July, 1995. That's when it was written. And it has to do with Srebrenica as well. Now, on this page it says "Military Assessment": "[In English] By attacking the Srebrenica enclave, the Bosnian Serb army probably wants to achieve the following aims: "Reduce the size of the enclave in order to be able to free assets for use in other -- in other conflict areas. Secure the road links to the north, south-east, and south-west of the enclave. [Interpretation] I'm going to miss one of them. "[In English] Eliminate the threat of the B and H harassment. Patrols, ambushes from the enclave, and increase the control over the enclave. Establish full control over the bauxite mine located on -- on this position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] All BSA offensive activity has been concentrated on the south-eastern part of the enclave and there are no reports of advances in other areas." [Interpretation] At the top it says that: "[In English] Having previously being prevented from withdrawing by the B and H -- was overrun by the B --" [Interpretation] All right, this doesn't matter. It has to do with the Dutch soldiers that were taken prisoner by the Muslims. We've already discussed that. So do you agree with the contention that General Janvier's assessment completely corresponds to the position of the Serb army to stop all links between Zepa and Srebrenica basically? Do you agree that General Janvier assessed that very accurately, the initial intentions of the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document, which was, it seems, sent on the 10th of July from Zagreb, so I would not have seen it at that time, this document gives what, in my view, is not a very appropriate assessment of the -- of the situation, and in general the -- if I can say so, the documents you have you've shown from General Janvier give a version of events which is very similar to how the Serbs were explaining it, but I think we saw it in more complicated terms. In particular, this document says that the Serbs probably wants to achieve the following aims: To reduce the size of the enclave. But this was written on Monday, the 10th of July. The enclave hardly existed on the Monday, the 10th of July. It had been reduced. Within just over 24 house of this, the entire enclave would be wiped out, but there's nothing in this assessment from General Janvier to Mr. Annan that says the Serbs may be intending to eliminate the entire enclave of Srebrenica even though by this point it's absolutely obvious that that's what they wanted to do. So with the fear of contradicting a military expert, I would say this assessment was proved to be dramatically factually incorrect within one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Sorry, what was General Janvier's position? I seem to have forgotten that.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you've -- you showed a piece of text that showed that he saw these -- ah, yeah, that it cannot be ruled out -- you -- you showed a document which said -- gave his assessment that the Bosnian government forces, the Bosniaks, the Muslims, were going to deliberately withdraw or pretend to collapse in order to provoke some sort of NATO response, and -- and that a -- that was -- and when you showed the document, I was able to confirm that was his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you say, We thought something different, what do you mean when you say "we"?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I thought something different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me remind you. General Janvier says here that actions are underway only at the south-east. That's the link between Zepa and Srebrenica; right? South-east is the link between Zepa and Srebrenica, and he says that that is the only place where there is activity and where there are some advances that are being made, and nowhere else. He is writing on the 10th about what he had received concerning the 9th; isn't that right? So what we see here is the situation on the 9th, because what is written on the 10th has to do with what happened on the 9th; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't see the reporting period, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 12.30 on the 9th -- on the 10th.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. By the 9th, the Dutch troops in Srebrenica were -- were so alarmed -- were alarmed enough by the posture of the Serbs and the advance of the Serbs that they had made five requests for air attacks, and the main request for air attacks by NATO was sitting on General Janvier's desk, and General Janvier never -- or did not approve those attacks, including up to the day before the fall of Srebrenica. And although I'm -- I may have seen this document before but I don't remember it, although -- and this document certainly gives his assessment, which is a substantial understatement of what the Serbs were attempt to do, in my view. It's by the way -- I mean, it is a small detail, it's not totally factually correct that the Serbs were only attacking from the south-east. By the 9th, they also controlled some high ground directly to the east. I forget the name of the place, Hotonj, or Hotolj or something. It begins with an H. But anyway, it's a detail. But certainly, I think, by this point it's absolutely obvious that they've gone beyond just clearing the road from Bosnian attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps it's better if I put specific questions so that you can just give yes or no answers. A witness from Srebrenica confirmed here that Srebrenica had not been defended. Do you agree with that? He said that it was actually abandoned on the 9th, which allowed the Serb forces to enter Srebrenica and that that was confirmed in a telegram that we are going to tender here one day, a telegram sent by General Tolimir to me asking whether they have approval to enter Srebrenica; that is to say that they had already left Srebrenica and stopped defending it. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, the Serbs attacked Srebrenica on the 6th -- on the enclave of Srebrenica on the 6th of July, and I think what you say may have been true after the 9th of July. I believe there was resistance from the 6th to the 9th, but then also in what you say is also what President Izetbegovic said, which is that the -- he was very surprised by the lack of Bosnian army defence, particularly after the 9th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like to remind you of something. Actually, I don't know whether you know about this. The position of the Serb side was to push them back to the agreed borders of the Srebrenica enclave. General Janvier perhaps assessed this on his own or had intelligence to that effect. Do you agree that the position initially was just to do that, not to take Srebrenica as such?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The attack began on the 6th. By the 7th, the Serbs were well within the area that had been demarked by General Morillon as on Bosniak territory, and then the Serbs continued to advance on the 7th, the 8th, the 9th, 10th; and then on the 11th, they overran the place completely. So I can't accept that statement, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We're going to prove that, that this action that General Janvier says was primarily on the south, that is to say between Zepa and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit this document now, unless it's already become a Prosecution exhibit? No? 981, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course no objection, Your Honour, but one question, actually. I'm just concerned about the continued reference to this as being General Janvier's report when I note on the first page of the document, although it might emanate from his office, it seems to have been drafted by a Major Bridge and the releasing officer was Colonel de Jonge, a G3.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That is for the Chamber to assess later. It will be admitted as?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D137, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I note that General Janvier also had his drafter, just like Mr. Harland was. When he was younger, I mean. 6D03. That's an old number. 981 is our number, but any way, it is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to draw your attention to the fact that it is already the 11th. Actually it says here the 10th of July, 1995, and this is being written to Mr. Akashi by Mr. Annan. And now I'm going to read the second paragraph. [In English] "In light of the serious attack by the B and H on the Dutch APCs, Riza called in the charge d'affaires of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ambassador Misic, and strongly protested the incidents. We emphasised that this action was particularly incomprehensible at a time when UNPROFOR had taken a clear and assertive position to respond with force against any further advance by the B and -- SA into the safe area of Srebrenica." [Interpretation] Do you agree that that attack on the Dutch APCs by the Muslim army had, as its ultimate objective, again a ploy to accused the Serbs? All of this was actually a ploy. There were a lot of war tricks being played around Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not sure I can agree with that. I think when the young Dutch soldier was killed my -- I interviewed some of the people on both sides around. I think it had been a sort of spontaneous act of sort of fear and anger by the -- by the Bosnian defenders. This -- this one I don't think was a -- I don't believe it was a trick. I also don't at all agree with this assessment from Mr. Annan, but that's a separate matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think there is no risk now to disagree with Mr. Annan because he's no longer in office.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Anyway, can we have this admitted. Can we admit this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D138.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I now have 1D954, please? This is a document from the Muslim side, from Zepa, dated the 5th of February, 1992, at the very outset, and down here the 30th of October, 1994. So that was 1995 and this is 1994. And now let's look at page 2. Do we have page 2? Yes, we do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, in the Serbian version it's the fourth paragraph. Various forms of disinformation. That is what it says in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you give me the date of this document again? The transcript says February 1992; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The first part up there is 1995, but this document is the 30th of October, 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There's also a mismatch between the Bosnian version and the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we see the first page of this document again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first document -- the first document is an accompanying letter. The 30th of January, 1995. The ministry is referring to a document dated October 1994. So the first part is a letter, and they are drawing the attention of the ministry to a letter from October 1994. So now this other document is 1994. If you agree, we are going to move on to page 2 now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We are trying to find a paragraph in English starting with, "Various forms of misinformation." You probably found it. Spread by people from Avdo's delegation have had repercussions on the situation in the Zepa Public Security Station. That's a police station, right? Particularly information on the disbanding of the Zepa SJB as well as information that so far, the 1st Zepa Light Brigade has received around 400.000 German marks and that this money is for the exclusive use for the brigade and it's members, while other organisations in Zepa have no resources at their disposal. And then further down in the penultimate paragraph it says: "The only thing that disturb the population was the conflict between the commander of the brigade here and the command of the 8th Operative Group regarding the way in which the Luka Company is operating. Luka is a locality. And the negotiations that were held by the commander of the brigade here at Bovsanica and what was discussed inter alia was the autonomy of Zepa in the so-called Republika Srpska." Do you agree that at the time Zepa was rather peaceful and that they could even negotiate about a secession of hostilities, however, Sarajevo never agreed to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit D139.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at 1D955, please. And while we're waiting, this is the Supreme Staff of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina sent to the 8th Srebrenica Group on the 9th of November, 1994. On the first page of the document, paragraph 1, the plan is -- in the English it's towards the bottom of the page: "The plan is --" "The plan is: Liberate in active combat actions part of the temporarily seized territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina - the municipalities of Bratunac, Vlasenica, Sekovici, Zvornik, and Kalesija, and link the free territories of Zepa and Srebrenica with the free territories of Zvornik, Kalesija, and Zivinice, in order to create a permanent free corridor for the supply of the population and logistics support to the units of the army of the RBH, and a basis for the further liberation of North-eastern Bosnia as a whole." At the United Nations were you aware that all the events in Srebrenica and Zepa were motivated with the idea of, as they term it, liberation of Eastern Bosnia and Herzegovina from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your first contention is certainly true, that the commanders of Zepa had a relatively professional relationship with the surrounding Serb units, and they sought a local cease-fire agreement. That was confirmed to me by Commander Palic himself, Avdo Palic. On the Srebrenica side, yes, it's certainly true. We were aware that the Bosniaks wanted to attack and were attacking sometimes out of the enclave. The nature of this document, however, is somewhat delusional. I mean, it wildly overstates what is possible or realistic military objectives for them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But this is sent by the Supreme Command Staff to Naser Oric as an instruction for further -- actually, Main Staff is stating its intentions to him. Wishes, intentions, however you want to put it.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit D140.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I have 1D956 now, please. While we're waiting, this is the 1st Zepa Light Brigade, and it's sending a telegram to Enver Hadzihasanovic, who is at the Kakanj command post, and it states: "Referring to your strictly confidential telegram with the above reference number, we inform you of the following: "Two sabotage operations were carried out in the Laze-Mislovo sector. The actions were carried out on the 12th of December, 1994. "We suffered no losses and had no wounded in these sabotage operations. "The Chetnik side had five killed -- five killed, one of whom was an officer." And it's signed by Colonel Avdo Palic. Would you agree that they should not have left the protected zone to go out and kill Serbs around it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say they should not have, I should remind you that according to our mandate, like it or not, that mandate was requiring all forces except for the Bosnian government forces to withdraw from around the -- the enclaves. Certainly it would have been useful if the sides had entered into a viable cease-fire, but our view was that neither side was interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We were interested. We could have used all those units around Srebrenica elsewhere. Isn't that right? Would you agree; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we're going to have to clarify this with some military expert about whether the protected zones should have been demilitarised or not. It is our view that they should have been demilitarised. Otherwise, how would it be possible for the Serb forces to withdraw while the Muslim side had all of these plans to liberate the entire area? So wouldn't you agree that there should have been no danger from without and from within the protected area; right? Would that make sense? Doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would agree that if this Resolution 824 and 836 which was basically directed against the Serb side, if it was going to be implemented it would have required vastly greater forces than were made available to UNPROFOR. So, yes, I think we can agree that there was a basic problem with -- with the mandate there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Harland, while the transcript is there, your answer to the previous question was, "Yes." I'm asking for the record.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The previous question, the one about --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters or the court reporter couldn't hear because you were overlapping.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "We could have used all those" -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and I would like to tender this document, please. And I would also like to call up 1D957.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted as.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D141, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the next document. I believe that we have it. Yes. We have both versions here. Actually, it's in English. I'm going to read it in English. This is also the 1st Zepa Light Brigade, and it says: On the 31st of December, 1994, addressed to Brigadier-General Enver Hadzihasanovic, and it states at the beginning: "[In English] Everything has been done on our part per your order and with a fair degree of success; the cargo was unloaded quickly, transferred to a secure location and the tracks covered. "UNPROFOR saw a helicopter entering the town and reported to the commander in Zepa that three helicopters had landed in the vicinity of Zlovrh (probably because they were circling during their descent). I made every effort to keep UNPROFOR from doing anything to harm us, and I will report on this to you when I have the time. This location for the helipad was suggested to you by Brigadier Naser Oric." Do you agree that Serbs do have cause for anger at the international community because not only are helicopters coming here, but it's also possible to ask the UNPROFOR commander not to take too much noise on this and to report back about it. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he doesn't say that he asks the UNPROFOR commander. At least in the English version he said he made every effort to keep UNPROFOR from doing anything to harm us. But certainly I can confirm and President Izetbegovic acknowledged it directly that the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina was very assertively violating the no-fly zone to insert weapons and sophisticated resent weapons and they told me -- President Izetbegovic told me, trainers as well and personnel, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, and I would also like to look at 1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. It will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D142, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next document is 1D958. I would also like to ask the witness, Mr. Harland, as well as you. We have a lot of documents confirm what has already been confirmed. Well, after this document. We're going to look at this document first, but there are several documents confirming the intense supplies of weapons and equipment to the enclaves in order to continue their military activities. Shall we go through them one by one, or can we just admit them in a bundle? Mr. Harland can also go through them one by one. It's up to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether Ms. Edgerton would agree with it.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I'd like a few moments to reflect on that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. You were informed of the kinds of exhibits Mr. Karadzic is referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes, and I've had a chance over the weekend to look at most of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's move on for the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have the document here, and routes and check-points in the area of responsibility of the Drina Corps. Convoys teams and individuals from UNPROFOR, the UNHCR, and the ICRC and humanitarian organisations entered the Drina Corps zone of responsibility and moved about therein on a daily basis during 1994 using the following roads and then the roads are referred to below. On the following page, following page --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Actually, are you familiar with the roads that are referred to on the first page, Karakaj, Zvornik, Bratunac, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: In general, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 now. We have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It states: "Behaviour and abuse of mandate by UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations?" And then second sentence: "They're particularly frequent on the routes to the Muslim enclaves of Srebrenica, Zepa, and especially Gorazde." And then the last sentence in that paragraphs: "Up to 30 transits by convoys, teams, and individuals are approved each day." So up to 30 a day, or as many as 30 a day, and we're going to see why. And then the following paragraph, no actually, we skip that one and then we look at the other one: "In 1994, as previously checks mostly revealed the following attempts at abuse: Transport of goods which are not permitted at all in UNPROFOR convoys, transport of goods which do not constitute humanitarian aid in convoys of humanitarian organisations, transport of goods in quantities greater than those permitted, attempts at border crossings without approval of the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska." Do you know that numerous convoys or a certain number of convoys committed such abuses?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Here is a point of disagreement: You said that the goods were not permitted at all. You permit -- you said that we were trying to cross the border without Bosnian Serb army approval, but we insisted on the principle of freedom of movement. So this document merely states that you had your position, but we had our position which was our mandate from the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But I think that there was no misunderstanding there between the UNPROFOR and the Army of Republika Srpska. A convoy had to be announced. The precise number of vehicles, precise number of personnel, and the type of goods; isn't that right? And it was understood that at least one inspection or check would be done? Do you agree? This was something that was agreed on.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serb side continuously abused the reasonable checks that we agreed to. We would agree to one check of large cargo vehicles as they entered Bosnian Serb army controlled territories, but this was constantly being abused. We have many orders from General Milovanovic saying we will not be allowed to move on Fridays, we will not be able to move without an additional inspection, we will not be allowed to carry radios in cars. There were extensive abuses of United Nations freedom of movement in Serb territory, the basic effect of which was to weaken UNPROFOR and to weaken humanitarian assistance in the enclaves that were inside Bosnian Serb held territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But General Wahlgren writes into a document that we're going to show here later, and also Mr. Akashi writes that Serbs were willing to allow the convoys pass but were making a lot of noise if we appeared at a different check-point or had an extra vehicle. Would you agree that a soldier who was informed at Karakaj that a convoy would cross there and the one at Cepi [phoen] has not informed about it, and then if the convoy appears at Sevka, the guy there cannot let it pass. And at Karakaj, if a convoy has 11 instead of 10 vehicles, the soldier cannot let it pass. Do you agree that somebody does not have the creative liberty to let through something that is not exactly as announced?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The Serbs never wanted to put in place a clear simple system that allowed us to have freedom of movement. They stole vehicles. They abused our people, they shot at our vehicles, and the document you're presenting does nothing except to confirm the very persistent bad behaviour, illegal behaviour of the Bosnian Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now we're going to see why that was. You say that there were no -- there was no smuggling and so on, and now we're going to look at the following paragraph. Actually, it's a paragraph in the middle: "There were such cases of the leaders of particular UNPROFOR convoys acting aggressively and threatening the VRS inspection organs, but they ceased after becoming aware of the determination of the inspection organs to carry out the blocking measures announced, in accordance with the instructions." And then the next paragraph: "Understandably, most cases of attempted smuggling of goods were in the convoys for Srebrenica, Zepa, and Gorazde, which had the fewest options for being provisioned. Apart from humanitarian aid, the following goods were those that were most smuggled, video cameras, cameras, film, weapons, radio sets, satellite equipment and antennae, signalling apparatus, optical devices, night vision apparatus, motor oil, various parts for devices, anti-freeze, chemical manoeuvre, oxygen cylinders, flack jackets, helmets, sleeping bags, military clothing and footwear, and various items of food. Articles of food were smuggled for the black market because their prices in the Muslim enclaves at one time were significantly higher, and goods for military purposes are the result of activities sympathetic to the Muslim side, in order to aid them in obtaining scarce goods for the requirements of the army. "There is no doubt that there would have been very few attempts to smuggle banned goods if those had been confiscated permanently at the check-points because temporary confiscation merely enforces delay and leaves the actors the hope that they will succeed in getting them to their destination at their next attempt, without any fear of the goods being permanently lost. "When representatives of UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations complain about the procedures of the organs at the check-points, in the majority of cases their aim is to use counter-accusations to lessen their own responsibility owing to attempts to abuse their humane function and play fast and loose with the mandate entrusted to them." Do you remember that goods were not permanently seized but they were temporarily confiscated and returned to those they were confiscated from upon their return?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The accusations made here are absolutely false. If we were bringing in video cameras, cameras, films, weapons, radio sets, satellite equipment, antennae signaling apparatus, optical devices, night vision apparatus, none of this ever appeared in the hands of the Bosnian government. We were bringing equipment for United Nations military personnel. When you say weapons, for example, you tried to stop the Dutch from bringing in their own 20-millimetre machine-guns that were the natural part of the armoured vehicles they had. You tried to stop us from bringing in the radios and the communications assistance. Was there some leakage from all of this onto the black market? Of the military equipment, in my experience, never or almost never -- I almost never found a Bosnian unit that had equipment that had come from us. I saw Chinese weapons. I saw many weapons, but not that. I would certainly agree that food aid was diverted partly to members of the fighting forces or to the black market, but basically these allegations are nonsense, and they are indicative of the differences that were between us then. I would say in answer to your last question that, no, in general when convoys were looted or pillaged by you, in general they did not give us back the equipment. In fact, I would often pass Serb -- through Serb facilities and find that they were driving our vehicles, vehicles stolen from us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Harland, that each such case was clarified between General Mladic and General Rose and later General Smith, but I don't see any reasons for you to get angry, because it's possible that you didn't know that. But this document is an internal army document. It's not propaganda. This is an internal army document where the commanders are informing each other about this. And later we're going to ask to have this document tendered. Now I want you to look at 1D967 so you can look at the Muslim sources discussing co-operation with certain branches of the UNPROFOR on the smuggling of very dangerous goods. 967, a document of the 23rd of February, 1996. There's a mistake in the date here. Can we look at page 4 of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's an analysis --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, did you want to comment upon the accused's statement that it was an internal army document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say that the -- the document is a perfect illustration of the massive violation by the Bosnian Serb side of the principle of freedom of movement which they kept affirming and reaffirming. I should make one small correction to the record, though. Where I said that I acknowledge that food aid would appear either with the Bosnian government forces sometimes or on the black market, the other item that would considerably appear in the black market would be fuel. But this list of materials they give was simply materials we had a minimal right to take for ourselves. And it's certainly not true what he says, that all these issues were resolved between General Mladic and General Rose and then between General Mladic and General Smith. We had hundreds of vehicles in the end that were stolen and not returned and many that were looted and the goods never recovered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1D958 will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D143, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Harland and the parties, please bear in mind that one of the members of the Bench is following the proceedings in French, which is much slower than English. So could you put a bit more pause than you would expect between the question and answers. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The document we have is an analytical overview about the conditions of the fall of Zepa and Srebrenica address to the commander of the Main Staff of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Rasim Delic, and it's sent by Jusuf Jasarevic, and this is now page 4 that we are going to look at. Actually, page 3 in English and page 4 in Serbian. It states: "Among the populations of Srebrenica, there is growing discuss trust towards the civilian and military leadership. There was all kinds of machinations with goods from humanitarian aid. As soon as Naser Oric and the municipal officials, Osman Suljic, Adem Salihovic, and Hamdija Fejzic were linked to this, there's information indicating that these men smuggled humanitarian aid, weapons, oil, and so on and so forth, and that they collaborated with members from UNPROFOR and even with the aggressor in their smuggling activities," meaning the Serbs. They're trying to say that it was with the Serbs. And then on the following page, and I can repeat that if necessary, but I think that you have it. And then it states on the next page: "During his time in Srebrenica, Oric surrounded himself with generally criminally-minded people such as Ejub Golic, commander of a battalion; Ibrahim Mandzic, aka Mrki; Husein Aljukic, aka Behaija; a man called Celo, who was his body-guard, and so on -- and others. These people committed several crimes at Oric's behest." And now, Mr. Harland, I believe that you didn't know about many things, but Muslim documents, many of them, some of which we're going to show you and some later, they received more food and more fuel than was needed, than was essential, that they smuggled these items, bought them from the United Nations, and that they also received and bought weapons from the United Nations. How are you going to explain, for example, that a convoy would have more of these flack jackets than there were UNPROFOR soldiers who would be using them, and did you believe that the Serbian Army did have reasons for concern knowing about the intentions of the commanders of those three protected areas to conquer or, as they say, liberate the entire North-eastern Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say that the Serbs were looking for excuses to strangle the enclaves. I have no doubt that there were criminal elements among the leadership on the Bosnian side. We were well aware of it. But it doesn't change the fact that the Serbs were massively interfering with our freedom of movement in order to reduce our effectiveness and in order to reduce the amount of humanitarian assistance that went to a deeply suffering population.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 6 and 5 in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for these pages to appear, Mr. Harland, how many convoys passed? For example, there were 30 a day headed for the enclaves. How many in total were recorded during the war? Discounting UNPROFOR convoys. How many convoys were sent in the direction of enclaves to provide for their needs? We're talking about thousands, are we not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The humanitarian situation was miserable. The people were cold and hungry. I don't have immediately the number of the convoys or of what they finally carried, but I can confirm to you that the situation, the basic situation of the ordinary innocent civilians was -- was miserable, and all the documents you've just shown simply confirm how you manipulated it to increase their misery.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We will see that that was not indeed the case. Things were different. I'm asking you how many convoys went to the enclaves throughout the war. Do you agree with me that over 10.000 planes landed at Sarajevo airport during the war?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably. That sounds about right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There was on average eight to nine a day; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably, until you ordered it stopped in early 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If it is convenient, shall we take a break now?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: May I ask you to go back to a general picture. There were 10.000 and even more flights landing in Sarajevo. Those aircraft were all within the range of Serb, Muslim, and other rifles, pistols. How many of the 10.000 flights experienced any problems at all from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: A relatively small number were -- were shot at and received bullets through the fuselage. Only one was shot down, I think, near the beginning of the war. I think that was by Croats, probably. And then sometimes we couldn't tell whether it was Serbs or Bosnians. A small number. I don't have the exact figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were right about that aircraft. That aircraft near Fojnica was outside of the range of Serb weapons. I agree with you. And now, throughout the 1.200 days or even longer while the enclaves of Gorazde, Zepa, and Srebrenica existed, how many convoys entered those enclaves, approximately?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thousands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How many experienced problems? You can almost list them. They were all recorded. They were wildly documented. CNN talked about them.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were problems big and small, but really we had a major problem and really a major problem with freedom of movement across Serb territory into the enclaves. I would say there was systematic interference both with UNHCR bringing humanitarian aid and with UNPROFOR trying to give itself the basic supplies. You yourself just mentioned the regular theft of flack jackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: First they would take them and then return them on the way back, but we'll come back to that. When it comes to the freedom of movement, we have information from UNPROFOR that when they passed through the Muslim territory then they would be in APCs and then when they reached the Serb territory they would get out. They would be out of the APCs because APCs used to be very uncomfortable and hot during the summer. Would you agree that they felt more at ease in the Serbian-controlled territories than they did in the Muslim-controlled territories?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would say first the most difficult places were always crossing the confrontation line. Second most difficult places were the internal check-points, including the Serb check-point at Rogatica was a major problem for us. But your general point that the Serb forces were more disciplined is, I think, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, let me try and put some numbers to the whole picture. Of the thousands of convoys, how many had to go back? I know of just one, in Rogatica. Women sent it back from Rogatica. As far as I know, all the others were able to pass through with or without problems or with some smaller or bigger problems. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We -- I -- this I insist on. There was a systematic attempt to block our freedom of movement, to limit the amount of humanitarian aid that reached the suffering populations and to allow UNPROFOR to do its job. It happened in Rogatica. It happened in Hadzici. It happened -- in the end, you closed down almost everything, and to get any convoys into Sarajevo or to resupply UNPROFOR we had to come over Mount Igman being shot at by your forces. So we have a different memory of the freedom of movement situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You will see that it was Muslim forces who opened fire, according to your sources and Muslim sources, but let's look at a document, and I'm reading -- this is the same document, Muslim analysis, which says: "At the time of Chetniks' attacks on Zepa on the 9th of July, 1995, about 6.500 people resided in the area. Just like the members of the 285th Light Brigade were well -- they were well supplied with all types of foodstuffs. In addition, information gathered to date indicates that the co-operation between civilian and military authorities of Zepa and the Ukrainian Battalion which was deployed in the Zepa sector was good up to the beginning of the beginning of the Chetnik offensive. After the commander of this UNPROFOR battalion crossed over to the Chetnik forces, meaning the Serb forces, the new commander of the Ukrainian Battalion handed over all the weapons at his disposal to our soldiers, and these were immediately used to defend Zepa. According to several displaced persons from Zepa, he even sent false reports to UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo saying that members of the Ukrainian Battalion had been directly attacked and requested NATO air-strikes against the Chetniks." Mr. Harland, do you see that the Muslim forces permanently resorted to all sorts of ploys, these ploys worked, and that's why we had to worry about the things that you might have had, because all those things could have been seized from you at any moment and sold on on the black market. Do you see the document? Do you agree with all that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this document says that he sent a false report to UNPROFOR command in Sarajevo. I was on the receiving end of that report, so I do recall receiving the report that weapons had been seized by the defenders. So maybe I was one of the ones who was deceived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that we can remove this document. However, I would like to say, Mr. Harland, that the concern on the part of one military about what UNPROFOR was in possession of, that could easily become the position of their enemy, the other military, is a legitimate concern. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no transfer of weaponry from UNPROFOR to the Bosnian forces directly. I mean, I can't say there was no -- absolutely zero criminal activity, but there was no significant element of that. What is true is that UNPROFOR was planning to directly use force against the Serbs, but only as a result of years and years of types of obstructions that you have just been illustrating.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to spare both you and the United Nations from showing some documents, both Muslim and yours. However, you called for it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be admitted, and can we now see 669 on our screens. P10669. 10669. I believe that it is already in evidence, and, Your Excellency, was the previous document admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 96 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 1D967 will be Exhibit D144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And was the Exhibit 65 ter number 10669, Ms. Edgerton? Do you follow?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour. I'm still on the last document, but I'll move with alacrity.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that's not it. 10669. That's the P number. P10669.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it has been admitted into evidence yet. My e-court says so. Let's proceed. Is that the right document, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. And this is its English version. And Oric's document has been admitted, the one in which he threatens that he will execute the prisoners. That was a long time ago, and that's only the Serbian version. And as for this document, we only have the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is your document. You drafted it together with Victor Andreev, or on behalf of Victor Andreev who sent it to Cedric Thornberry. Let's look at the last paragraph on page 1. I'm going to read in English: [In English] "The inference of organised crime appeared to have reached unprecedented levels especially in Sarajevo." You recognise your own words, don't you.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the top of the second page, please, starting with the "Rump B and H." I will need the entire page, but for the time being, let it be like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English] "Muslim radicals appear to be gaining the upper hand at the expense of moderates who favour a multinational B and H society. BH controlled Sarajevo is approximately 80 per cent ethnic Muslims -- Muslim. The non-Muslims are being replaced in government by Muslims, and non-Muslims are increasingly uncomfortable. "Organised crime appears to be spiraling out of control in Sarajevo. UNPROFOR has been drawn into the problem - its personnel and facilities being used as conduits for black market goods. Civil affairs personnel have also been touched (the local Mafia have evicted Daljeet Bagga from his apartment at 5 minutes' notice; threatening calls have been made to civil affairs by black marketeers wanting press cards)." [Interpretation] Mr. Harland, I think that at that time you were a lot less biased than you are today in the courtroom, and in here you qualify the situation in Sarajevo without painting a rosy picture or hedging unnecessarily. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not. My position is not much different from when it was. I just don't think that the criminalised element of what was going on in Bosnian government territory justified any of the terrible things happening on the other side. I was equally critical I like to think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And can we scroll down and start reading from the paragraph beginning with "The food situation": [In English] "The food situation continues to be confusing. Convoy deliveries have increased recently, but the distribution by the BH government to Sarajevo citizens is still very limited. Large quantity, this food is diverted to the military and a smaller amount re-surfaces on the black market. The bulk of the missing aid (perhaps 60 per cent), remains unaccounted for. Speculation is that the BH government is stockpiling it." [Interpretation] Do you remember this part of your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a statistician working on this problem, but I must say we even didn't get so much co-operation from UNHCR in our investigations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's why I'm saying that you don't have to defend yourself, because you did not have to know everything, but we knew it. Do you agree that we knew how well supplied they were?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm -- I don't know, but I can believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be admitted into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note that's one of the documents proposed by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Quite so, Your Honour. Quite so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be admitted as part of Prosecution exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P830, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are for another document, can we go back to the previous document which was admitted as Exhibit P144 or 1D00967. While that document will be appearing in our monitor, Mr. Karadzic, I noted that the date on the cover page seems somewhat odd, as it is dated as -- as February 1995 while dealing with the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the beginning, I said that there is a printing error. It is obviously the year 1996, February 1996. There's a typo in the document. This is a subsequent analysis of the fall of the enclave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, which document did you say that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Move on to your next topic. I wanted just clarify this date.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce 09599, just briefly. I'm interested in one paragraph only. Yes. Very well. And in this document I'm interested in page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This document, as we can see, was drafted by yourself, and Mr. Andreev sent it to Cedric Thornberry, according to a customary procedure. This is one of the more common documents and let's read from the paragraph starting with the BM media. That's 1, 2, 3, 4, 5th paragraph from the top of the page. "[In English] [Overlapping speakers] The BH media is bringing the UN for many of its wars, including organised crime. Ukrainian and French troops allegedly conduct a wide range of black market and other illegal activities in Sarajevo, often in full view of the Sarajevo public. The allegation may be well-founded."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "[In English] BH snippers have been firing on UN personnel and around UNPROFOR's forward headquarter. Two Bosnian snippers have been firing, not only at the UN personnel, but also at local pedestrians in the vicinity. First call claimed that these snipers are renegades, supporters of Caco."

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The small number of maybe 1 or 2 per cent of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, you're so fast the interpreters missed your question. As a result. It was not translated. Although Mr. Harland was able to answer. What was your question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question was whether he remembers this report, the report about those events. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm not attacking either you or the United Nations. However, we can see from all of those examples that the Serbian military did have a good reason for concern and that it had to take into account and be fully aware of what was being supplied to the other side. And according to our estimates, there was plenty of food, but the food was abused, sold on the black market, and that the high stations of power participated in that. Would you agree that all of the above arises from your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't agree that all the above arises because of my report. I would say yes it is true that there was some black market activity, including by some members of UNPROFOR. For example, the selling of fuel, diesel fuelling from the Ukrainian base headquarters in Sarajevo. I would acknowledge that. But the overall situation was one of extremely limited food and other necessities of daily life caused by the -- the siege. You didn't ask any question about the second paragraph you read, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This talks about sniping activities against UNPROFOR and their own civilians. According to the 1st Corps, those were renegades which supported Caco. That was the answer given to you by them; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what they told us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you will probably remember that Caco was under the direct command of Alija Izetbegovic, who even visited him in his headquarters, as we will see in some of the documents; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that Caco was under the control of anybody during this rather wild phase of September and October of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be admitted, Your Excellency. What did you say about one of the previous documents? You said something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is also included in the Prosecution's list and has been admitted already. And the number is?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document has been admitted as Exhibit P823.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Harland, I would like to go briefly to -- through some documents speaking about the armament of the enclaves. We don't have to see all of them, but we don't have to waste a lot of time. I would like to call 1D959. While this is being produced, I would like to introduce it to you. This is a report, a text, rather, which was submitted to the 8th OG in Srebrenica, to the attention of Naser Oric, and it was sent by General Hadzihasanovic on the 2nd of February, 1995. 1D959.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for the English version, I'm going to read in Serbian. "Immediately arrange for the reception of the helicopter at the agreed location (building fires) and so on and so forth.
