This shipment will be delivered by helicopter in two rounds and it shall be distributed as follows:" And now there's a list of all the ammunition and equipment that they will be provided with. Do you see the document, and do you agree that that's exactly how things transpired?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see the document. I can't confirm this specific document, but it generally accords with our understanding of how weapons were transferred into Zepa and Srebrenica, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps we can move a bit faster now.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm surprised how cigarettes got on the list of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be Exhibit D144.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it should be 145?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, 145.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Exhibit D145.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D961, please. Then 962, so that we can move fast. This is in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So on the 13th of February, 1995, yet again this is a report concerning 150 rifles, RPGs for Srebrenica, Zepa, and also it says: "Rifles are to be handed over to the indicated manoeuvre brigade, the money, 3.000, 8.000 German marks that Brgulja took over from the pilot is to be handed over to the OG-8 Srebrenica Command." Do you see this document? Does that fit into what you knew?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can it please be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Ms. Edgerton, you have an observation.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, no objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, it will be Exhibit D146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And do you have objection to 1D962?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 1D962 will be Exhibit D147, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did UNPROFOR try to control this influx of weapons and military equipment into Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had a -- a so-called no-fly zone policy, and we did have an arrangement with NATO which gave them a general authorisation to intercept and destroy non-cleared aircraft, but it was very easy for helicopters on short flights to evade the no-fly zone or to evade detection and interception.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a similar document dated the 16th of February. This is a third flight into Zepa in the month of February carrying a lot of weapons, and it says here: "The shipment that was announced has arrived. "The aircraft has been hit and is now in Zepa. You or your deputy should come, if you can, with your men to take it over and to clarify some issues on the spot. Do it when I send you the signal Mjesec. That's a code isn't it. Do not send anyone now before the aircraft takes off. For security reasons, be very cautious of UNPROFOR, the column with the cargo should absolutely move at night only. The previous group was detected by UNPROFOR with all the cargo and manpower between Vukoljin Stan and Sarena Bukva." So you seen how intensive the arming was in February, the arming of Zepa and thereby Srebrenica as well. Do you agree that this had to alarm the Serbian Army to the effect that something was in the making?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a considerable movement of weaponry, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted into evidence. Oh, it already has been admitted. 1D965. Could that please be admitted or, rather, could that be called up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is information by way of a response signed by Brigadier Naser Oric. General, rather. And he is sending it to the Main Staff, to Enver Hadzihasanovic, and he said that command of the Srebrenica OG has recently received the following materiel and technical equipment in Zepa and delivered it to Srebrenica as per your memo, et cetera, et cetera. And then there's a list of everything they received over that period of time. This is the 17th of February. You see that there is ammunition here, mines, 60 millimetres, cables for tank crews, hand grenades. There are cigarettes too. Not that many, but yes. Anyway, do you agree that all of this happily arrived in Zepa and Srebrenica and was ready to be used against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't confirm this exact document or shipment, but it generally accords with our understanding, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that UNPROFOR was, in all fairness, supposed to prevent that arming of Zepa and Srebrenica? Somehow the Muslims succeeded to do this, during the night or whatever, as if there weren't any restrictions; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The previous document, in fact, confirms one of the Bosnian commanders expressing great anxiety because UNPROFOR was interdicting the material. To your second question, I would simply say I think you and I both know who was the main violator of the free -- the no-fly zone, and a relatively small number of Bosnian flights escaped, but not nearly as many as those of your own.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's a bit tu quoque, as we say; right? But it is a fact -- well, I'm not saying that UNPROFOR allowed it, but they nevertheless did succeed in deceiving UNPROFOR and arming Zepa and Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zepa and Srebrenica were, by the moment they fell, not at all well armed from what our personnel in Srebrenica and Zepa could see. It's certainly true that some material got through, but they were not well armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But in one of the previous documents, an analysis of the fall of Zepa, they say that they had enough food, enough ammunition, and in addition to that they took the weapons of the Ukrainian Battalion; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think both in Srebrenica and in Zepa the defenders had small arms, not enough for every soldier, but they had small arms and they had ammunition. President Izetbegovic expressed to me his frustration that they weren't able to use effectively the few medium weapons they had, the antitank rockets and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, he did admit to you that he sent sophisticated weaponry to Zepa and Srebrenica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has this document been admitted, 962?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. 965. Actually, I'm asking for 968 to be called up in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 1D965 will get admitted as?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D148, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the next document, Mr. Karadzic, I'm of the opinion, of the view that all of these facts, in particular relating to the arming of the Srebrenica or Zepa enclave, would not be objected to by the Prosecution, so you may wish to think about sitting yourself, or your legal advisors may sit with the Prosecution and discuss and produce all the agreed facts. That will save us a lot of time. The Chamber is minded to arrange a kind of 65 ter meeting in which we'll encourage the parties to agree upon as many facts as possible. So think about it, and let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's not that they sat and discussed this, but they did discuss it over the break on their feet. The Prosecution wanted these documents to be shown nevertheless. 968, 967, 970, 971, 972, all of these documents speak of significant quantities of weapons and ammunition, and it's regular. On the 25th of February, and sophisticated weaponry, rockets, RPGs, nitroglycerine, ammunition for breaking fortifications, and so on. All of this indicates that there was a great deal of activity going on. One of the dates is the 4th of March. Then also mines. 82 millimetre, 60 millimetres, launchers. 971 on the 21st of April, also lots of ammunition. On the 27th of April as well. Significant quantities of weapons and ammunition. If you agree, if everyone agrees, the Trial Chamber, the Prosecution and the witness, all of these documents could be admitted into evidence because they are authentic and they show this exceptional rhythm of arming Zepa and Srebrenica. And in the summer of 1995, it will become evident that all of that was done with the objective of starting an offensive from these enclaves. Can we agree on having all of these documents admitted? They all speak of the same thing, but it's just a question of rhythm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. That's not quite consistent with the very brief discussions that we had with Mr. Sladojevic during the break. We indicated we wanted to see the documents at issue, and we certainly agreed to look them over and accepted the possibility of agreeing to their admission but not before we had a chance to hear which ones were at issue and what the proposed relevance in. In general, we -- we're happy to follow the guidance of the Court as recently -- as just enunciated a few moments ago. So, no, we didn't reach an agreement on the admission of those documents. I accept it certainly in principle that possibility, but we indicated clearly to Mr. Sladojevic, who I think understood and agreed with that approach, that we'd have an opportunity to see which ones they had in mind and look them over quickly first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The issue was not whether there was an agreement but you would -- but whether or not you were opposed to the admission of those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER

I noticed that he was receiving directly by convoy from Sarajevo a quantity of goods, fuel, and footwear which our unit needs." So this person is some kind of sheik in Zepa. He has his own clothing and fuel supplies, and all of this is going through -- passing through the check-points unimpeded. But you also have stated that you were conducting investigations about this just like the Serbian side was. But anyway, this is a Muslim document. This is not a document that was drafted by the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm we were conducting our own investigates, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document please be admitted into evidence. Or, rather, can it be MFI'd, because a translation is still pending.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Unless it is objected to, it will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D159, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And that said, we will have a break for an hour, but before that, Mr. Robinson, the document we admitted minutes ago which was admitted P831 which has the 65 ter number 21139, was one of the documents you're opposed to. At that -- am I correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's correct. That is on the list, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the point of your position while using as Defence exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, at the time based on the foundation that was laid in the 65 ter amalgamated statement, we felt that it fell without -- or outside of the Trial Chamber's ruling, but since it's been further identified and discussed by the witness, it seems like it can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We will have an hour. We will convene again at half past 1.00, and in the afternoon instead of half an hour break we will have a three-quarters break, 45 minutes. So today we will end about a quarter past 5.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's begin. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for Prosecution 10820, Prosecution number. Could I have that in e-court. Dated the 13th of June, 1995. Do we have it on the screens? No, we don't. Yes. Yes, there is an English version too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I would like to draw your attention to this order which I had issued to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska on the basis of the conclusions of the State Committee for Co-operation with the UN and international humanitarian organisations, and then we actually see the order. Actually, I can read this part in Serbian: "To allow the UNHCR to occasionally, according to notifications, lead a humanitarian convoy from Metkovic to Trebinje and from Metkovic to Sarajevo along the road marked as safe by the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska (via Herzegovina and Trnovo or via Kiseljak and Ilidza, and by no means via Hadzici or Ilijas). For this particular week, the convoy Metkovic-Trebinje and Metkovic-Sarajevo should be approved according to the notification. "2. In relation to the incident concerning the ammunition found in the UNHCR convoy for Zepa and Gorazde, a detailed investigates should be allowed for a commission involving Milos Dzurdzic, an officer from the Main Staff, Momcilo Mandic, and Dragisa Mihic." That is to say military security, then public security, rather the minister of justice and Dragisa Mihic, deputy head of state security. "The task of the commission is to submit a detailed report to the state committee for relations with the UN and international humanitarian organisations." You will recall that the chairman of the committee for relations with the UN was the vice-president of the republic, a renowned professor, a specialist for Shakespeare, Professor Nikola Koljevic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could I have appointed a more eminent person at a higher level than that? Could it have been anyone else but the president of the republic then? So it was the number two man in the country who was appointed.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was vice-president, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. All of this can be seen. The entire document can be seen [No interpretation]: "[In English] A positive opinion [indiscernible] three should be immediately given to all the notifications that arrived through the co-ordination body for humanitarian operations attached to the state committee, referring to weekly plan -- to the weekly plan of deliveries of the UNHCR from 10 to 17 June, that have already been examined by the committee. "To allow ICRC to continue its visit of imprisoned members of UNPROFOR except those in housed -- that are housed in critical locations, to allow ICRC to leave Sarajevo, to allow passage to the ICRC," and so on. [Interpretation] I would now like to draw your attention to the date, the 13th of June, 1995. So this Directive 7 was that relevant. It had no effect. Can't you see? This is an explicit order to the Main Staff, and it was observed for the most part, and Vice-President Koljevic enjoyed quite a bit of respect, and he was quite influential too. So it's not that any non-commissioned officer could oppose what he had to say. Wouldn't you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't think he had much influence over the military structures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. This is a Prosecution number, isn't it? Can it be admitted, this order?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think this is included in one of the exhibits on the part of the Prosecution. As well, it is one of the documents listed by Mr. Robinson to be opposed to. However, we will admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this will be Exhibit P832.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, during the course of questioning Mr. Karadzic said to the effect that in light of this document, the Directive 7 was not that relevant, or to that effect. It had no effect. Do you have any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The document, which I've never seen before, so I can't comment on its authenticity, is extremely interesting. One, because it openly acknowledges they are holding large numbers of UNPROFOR prisoners, hostages, and it's allowing people -- it's allow the ICRC to visit them. I mean, so the document is extremely illustrative of the situation in which the way the Serbs were behaving. I would say that in the opening in chief, I said that the Serbs tended to suddenly reduce the pressure on us and reduce the amount of shelling and sniping and killing and allow more food to go through when they were under threat, and there was a particular moment here, this is after -- I think we made some air attacks on them at the end of May, and they were very -- they then seized some hostages, a large number of hostages, and there was a threat of a major escalation, and this is precisely an example of how they were trying to de-escalate so as not to get into a conflict with NATO while admitting they had a lot of hostages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm not going to thank you for that analysis. Let the Trial Chamber thank you because they're there for that. It's their job, isn't it. However, 10669, this document that we saw earlier on, the date is October 1993. We allowed these convoys again: [In English] "The convoys delivered having cleared [indiscernible] recently but distribution by the B and H government to Sarajevo citizens," [Interpretation] and so on and so forth. That was not provided to the people. In this case, the bombing was already over, and while we were hosting the UNPROFOR people, and you call them hostages but we are going to oppose that with arguments, during that period of time there was no danger of us being bombed. So this order was a sign of goodwill rather than of fear, but let it be.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Oh, actually, this has already been admitted; right? It's part of something, isn't it? Oh, I see. That's the document that this is. I just wanted to mention -- actually, can we have the document that's here. The one that's here has already been admitted. Could we just have page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I note this was admitted as P -- Exhibit P830.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I just wanted to remind Mr. Harland of the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In Sarajevo, et cetera, and organised crime, and then the one where it says the food situation, et cetera. So there was no bombing. There was no threat of bombing at that point in time. And we let these people through. However, Mr. Harland, arithmetic shows that thousands of convoys had passed and only a few had problems, and that thousands of aircraft landed and that less than ten had some problems. So this is a vast disproportion between those that did run into problems and those that did not; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The document we were looking at from sometime in the middle of June, I think, of 1995, by that time your forces had tried to completely seal and strangle Sarajevo. And I don't know what happened that week, but basically nothing came into Sarajevo during that late spring and summer except what we were able to fight over Bosnian government controlled territory through firing from your guns in Ilidza. So it was -- very few convoys came in. The statistics will show almost nothing, except what we were able to fight through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now it's the Muslim government that would have to thank you. However, do you remember that that summer, already by mid-June, there was this huge offensive launched by the Muslim side that had been prepared for a long, long time; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So it's the fault of the offensive. It's not our fault. Do you perhaps have the report in which you characterise the shelling of Sarajevo on the 16th or the 17th of June? That is to say, a few days after this, how you counted these shells and who you ascribed them to, as it were. Do you have that report?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the first part of your question, I don't think it's true that we can blame the offensive. In fact, I don't think that because there was a Bosnian government offensive - which is correct, you are correct - I don't believe that's a reason to inflict additional suffering on the civilian population. In fact, it's that concern that principally brings me here. Concerning your second question about how to characterise the shelling of Sarajevo on the 16th or 17th of June, I can't remember. I think this was the period of those sort of improvised rockets, wasn't it, in the middle of June, just after the Bosnian offensive. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, now we would have to go back to one of the previous documents that clearly states - it is your document - that they had enough food but that they had stockpiled it somewhere. They didn't give it to the people. So there was food, but they're the ones that caused the suffering. The Muslim side hid that food in order to keep prices high and in order to victimise Sarajevo. May I ask you how much time is needed to prepare that kind of massive offensive? That certainly could not have been done over three or five days. It must have been prepared for months; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was prepared long in that sense, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I now call up 038320.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is another document of yours. I think that 0383 is -- 03832, actually. 03832, that's a Prosecution number, isn't it? And the date is the 19th of July, 1995, and it has to do with the proposed demilitarisation of Zepa. You were with General Smith then. This is the first page. And Security Council Resolution 998 is being referred to.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 2, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it in English. We don't have a translation: [In English] "We recommended that UNPROFOR propose an immediate and complete demilitarisation of the Zepa safe area, to be implemented under UNPROFOR supervision within 48 hours of agreement (in accordance with Reference C)." [Interpretation] Reference C is Resolution 998 from page 1. Resolution 998 envisages demilitarisation, that is. Then in the second paragraph: [In English] "The draft agreement should be presented first to the Bosnian government and then to the Bosnian Serb authorities." [Interpretation] Then further on: [In English] "The Bosnian government accept the agreement and the Bosnian Serbs refused. Pale will be informed that under Resolution," so and so, "military assets, as well as the direct and essential military support facilities, including but not limited to fuel installations and munitions sites will be subject to NATO air-strikes (Reference to D and E Resolution)." [Interpretation] Actually -- actually, when NATO decided that [indiscernible]. And then there's Akashi's telegram to Annan in April. Do we agree now that there is a prerequisite for bombing the Serbs? That is to say that Zepa is demilitarised and the Serbs are still targeting Zepa, and they have military equipment around it; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were trying to clarify the exact circumstances that might give rise to air attacks. This is, of course, something we were drafting just a week or so, I think, after the fall of -- of Srebrenica. So we were extremely worried about the situation in Zepa, and we -- and this is an example of how we were trying to prepare, including to use airpower more effectively.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All of that is to be commended, but the point is that Serbs could not be bombed before the enclaves -- or, rather, the safe areas are demilitarised in accordance with Reference C, that is to say Security Council Resolution 998, which provided for demilitarisation. We were bombed, though, although none of these demilitarised -- these safe areas had been demilitarised. On the contrary. The Secretary-General informed the Security Council that the safe areas are military strongholds. So the point here is not your noble attentions but what the precondition was for bombing the Serbs. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The preconditions for the circumstances in which the Serbs could be bombed are outlined in Resolution 836. The problem is that 836 is not very precise. So this is one example by me of a proposal by me to my boss to give great precision to the end transparency to the sides about precisely when we might use overwhelming force, because we felt that if this had been clearer in Srebrenica, then we might have been able to avoid the outcome there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A wonderful line of thinking. However, unfortunately the Muslim side did not accept that. Could we see page 3 now where we see the draft document for the demilitarisation of Zepa is that you had proposed within this effort. I'm going to read out the second paragraph: [In English] "No later than 12 hours after the signature of this agreement, all firearms and munitions (regardless of calibre) in the possession of the Bosnian Army or others within the Zepa safe area shall be turned over to the UNPROFOR UKRBAT in Zepa. These weapons shall be destroyed by UNPROFOR at the earliest feasible opportunity in the presence of observers from both parties." Do you believe, as I do, that this is a good proposal? Do you think that it came in too late? Had it come in earlier, everything would have been different.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's my proposal, so I can't obviously say it's not a good proposal. The basis on which we could use force is Resolution 836, which imposes certain obligations on the Bosnian Serb party. It does not, if I remember correctly, unilaterally require a demilitarisation. Yes, a demilitarisation would have made it much easier. And this was negotiated in the context of the fact that the Bosnian commander in Zepa, Colonel Palic, though he was not supported by Sarajevo, I think, was willing to consider an agreement like this. And he went directly to negotiate with General Tolimir and General Mladic about it, but when he went to do so, they took him away and then he was killed. So this agreement never came to a good outcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, I have to correct you with regard to the sequence of events. Something had happened to him even earlier.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But can we -- can this document please be tendered into evidence before that?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's one of the associated documents to this witness's statements, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Yes. Referred to in paragraph number 223.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. It will be admitted as Prosecution can be.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P833, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce 993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And before that, let me ask you, Mr. Harland. Do you remember that I, on several occasions, from 1992 up until the end of 1994 proposed for Sarajevo to be demilitarised [Realtime transcript read in error "militarised"] and proclaimed an open town and placed under the control of the United Nations? There are a lot of documents to the effect, but I'm asking you whether you remember that that's indeed the fact.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And can I say that the text you just showed is really an example of how we, even me who you clearly think was not very sympathetic to your position, was making really a good effort to try to stabilise the situation around the safe areas and were really considering force really as the -- only as the last resort. But I can confirm that I was at meetings from the Igman period on where you supported a total demilitarisation of Sarajevo and other enclaves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I really don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Line 6, militarised should read demilitarised, for the record. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I really don't have any doubts about your good intentions, but the problem was, according to a very imminent witness, you were evidently on the Muslim side. Wasn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What an unkind witness. Who was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A very imminent witness, and you co-operated with him. What you just said about Palic prompted me to use the following document. I don't know whether there is a translation. Let me read: "Smith stated that our side, which is the Muslim side, did not accept the -- the agreement on exchanges all for all and that our side was asking for additional concessions. In Boksanica, which was the place of negotiations, Hamdija Torlak stayed behind, and he was told that if we were prepared to carry out the exchange, General Smith should be informed during the night so that a plan of helicopter evacuation could be drafted. President," that's Mr. Izetbegovic, "on behalf of my brigade, which is on the brink of a nervous breakdown, I implore you to do everything in your power for our side to accept that agreement. And finally the [indiscernible] of our hardships. We cannot believe that it is you who do not want to solve the problem." This corroborates what you have just said, and it also corroborates our thesis, and that is that Mr. Izetbegovic augmented the suffering of his people in order to provoke a military intervention on the part of the West. Is that what you meant when you said that Palic had not had support in his efforts to strike a deal with the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel Palic, who I had met sometime before, had always favoured an early negotiated end to the conflict, and he wanted to set a good example in the area around Zepa. By this stage Srebrenica had already fallen. Very large numbers of people had been massacred. Zepa, which was a very small community, was being attacked and was about to collapse, and Colonel Palic told us that he wanted quickly to reach a negotiated conclusion, but this was not accepted by President Izetbegovic. We put it to President Izetbegovic, and when he tried to negotiate it directly with the Serbs, even under a flag of truce, it seemed that they -- they killed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know exactly how he was killed, but it is well known that it was after all the negotiations and after the evacuation of Zepa. But let me ask you, do you remember that the Army of Republika Srpska did have a lot of reasons not to trust Mr. Palic, because the convoy that supplies the relay in 1992, in May or in June, had been massacred, although Avdo Palic had given his word that he would secure the relay. However, young men from Pale and elsewhere were burnt there. Do you think that they should have trusted him again, although the previous experience that they had -- had with him was awful? Wouldn't that have been a good reason for concern when it came to any deals and negotiations with Palic? What do you think?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That occurred before I was there. While I was there, the Serb's military around Zepa had a reasonably professional relationship with him. General Tolimir then said at this point that he was willing to negotiate with Colonel Palic. I was not there, but my colleague Ed Joseph escorted him up to the check-point where he would -- could negotiate this agreement with General Tolimir under a flag of truce. General Tolimir had him taken away, and his body, dead body, was only identified much, much later. I think it's really a terrible thing that your forces did to -- to Palic under a flag of truce.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document, Palic's telegram, if it's not already, can it be, Palic's telegram, what is on the screen, can it be admitted into evidence, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Do we have the English translation? Not yet. It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D160, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, we were talking about the Zepa negotiation. In the course of answering you said at one point, By this time Srebrenica had fallen and a large number of people had been massacred, or to that effect.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My question is when was it known to you that that took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we were aware that Srebrenica had fallen straight away. I believe that the first survivors of the massacre appeared in Bosnian government held territory around the 18th. There is one -- the very first person which led me to send an officer from my office to investigate first made a statement on television that -- Bosnian government television that there had been a massacre. We didn't know anything about it then because the Serbs were negotiating with us for a prisoner exchange. So we were a bit skeptical, but we sent people to investigate, and then later, several months later, I myself went to investigate some of these sites. So we were just beginning to be aware in this period that a large-scale massacre had taken place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D984 is the document that I would like the court to produce now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It's another telegram sent by Colonel Palic. He sent that telegram to Asim Dzambasovic, a brigade general, asking him to forward the telegram to Dr. Heljic as urgently as possible. And now let's look at the reference UNPROFOR. If this can be blown up a little, we will be able to see it. He says: "UNPROFOR, we are disarming UNPROFOR according to the previously given instructions. That was on the 16th of July. We are disarming UNPROFOR according to the previously given instructions." And that was sent to the General Staff of the army in Kakanj, to the administration for operative planning, to Brigadier Asim Dzambasovic personally. You see, you did not have a very easy time with them either, did you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] we also had our --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can 984 be admitted, please. And can we now be provided with 06864, the Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Now it's -- could you repeat your answer, because your answer was not recorded in full because the microphone was not activated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I said, yes, we also had our difficulties, I think.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Has the previous one be given a number? Has it been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This will be admitted again. Exhibit D161.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 06864, Prosecution document, was drafted by you and by Mr. Andreev on the 28th of September, 1994. And it was sent to the late Sergio de Mello, who -- who got killed in Afghanistan, unfortunately, in Iraq, okay. On page 1, Pale meeting. I will proceed in English: [In English] "Dr. Karadzic and his colleagues Professor Koljevic, Mr. Krajisnik, General Milovanovic began the meeting in Pale with an angry statement about the Bosnian attack out of Sarajevo on Sunday, 18th of September, 1994. Karadzic said that there could be no talks on demilitarisation after such attack and that he would flatten the Presidency if there were a repetition of the episode." [Interpretation] Do you think that they had the right and they did good for both sides when we were in the middle of negotiations about the demilitarisation of Sarajevo that they launched fierce attacks around Sarajevo? Would you say that that was a peace-loving effort or was it a warmongering effort? What would you say.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't sound like a peace-loving initiative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you can we now see the following page, which describes your meeting with Izetbegovic. Number 7, paragraph number 7: [In English] "President Izetbegovic was absolutely contrite with Sunday's attack, and promised, in front of General Delic, that there would be no repetition of the incident." [Interpretation] Mr. Izetbegovic accepted responsibility and he promised that that was the end of that. However, as we know, that wasn't the end. Do you remember that meeting with Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't now remember exactly the meeting or the attack, but it certainly is part of a familiar pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know whether you believed him, but let me tell you that we doubted all of his promises.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see page 3 in the same document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Conclusions," number 10: "On the brighter side one would have to conclude that General Rose's swift actions in denouncing the Bosnians for Sunday's attack was a success. His comments threatened to undermine their vital advantage, international sympathy and support through positive media coverage. If they undertake similar provocative actions in the future, then I think that they will at least be careful to disguise them better." [Interpretation] And then paragraph 11 your remarks about the Serbs: [In English] "With the Serbs things are much less positive. The Serbs feel cornered by the closing of the border with FRY. If more sanctions are imposed on them there will certainly be a back-lash about -- both on the Bosnians and on us." [Interpretation] You appropriately estimated that the Muslims benefitted from short but very fierce attacks. On the other side, you realise that we were cornered by various problems, including sanctions and so on and so forth, can you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This doesn't look like a pro-Muslim assessment. Did I draft this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. You drafted this, but you said that their attack was a success because they gained --

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. It looked very balanced, very correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, our backs were breaking at the time. The Serb backs were breaking, but that was your position. Let's look at number 9 on the same page: [In English] "The president asked General Rose whether or not the Serbs had agreed to restore gas, electricity, and water to the city. The general informed him that the Serbs had agreed on the condition that the Bosnian side co-operated with the restoration of utilities elsewhere in the country." [Interpretation] Do you remember that General Rose accepted my offer and he thought that it was fair, but there was a condition or a question why Gornji Vakuf or Sebobrin [phoen] would not have water at the same time because there were people living there as well. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember the linkage of Sarajevo with Donji Vakuf, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a Prosecution document. Can it been tendered into evidence or has it already been admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit it as a Prosecution exhibit because it is included in the associated exhibit list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will Exhibit P834.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the court please produce 1D -- oh, it hasn't arrived yet. It hasn't been uploaded in e-court. Can I offer an excerpt from General Rose's book, "Fighting for Peace." The Prosecution should have it already. Does the Trial Chamber need this, a copy? Does the witness need a copy as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While the copies are being distributed by way of an introduction let my say this: Mr. Harland, in one of your statements, you recorded my anger about some things that had happened in September 1994. However, I'm still not clear on one thing. You said that I was angry and that I threatened, but you left it as my final word, not as my introduction into our entire conversation. Do you remember that? Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In any case, the Prosecutor may have been using only the part that they find useful. In any case, it -- according to what you stated, it seems that it was my final decision to introduce restrictions. But let's see what General Rose, Michael Rose, has to say on page 174 of this document which hasn't been uploaded in e-court, but maybe it can be placed on -- very well. But it doesn't have to go on the ELMO. It doesn't have to be put on the ELMO, but maybe for the audience, yes, yes: [In English] "There was a limit to the hard line that we could take with the Bosnian government. They knew that the Americans were unlikely to allow NATO airpower to be used against the Bosnian army even though it was in breach of a NATO ultimatum, nor was it likely that economic sanctions would be imposed on the Bosnians for breaking UN Security Council resolutions. In this context, UNPROFOR was not able to sustain the principle of impartiality that is so essential to any peacekeeping mission." [Interpretation] Do you agree that this is just another way of putting that you were overwhelmingly on the Muslim side? And I don't mean just you personally but the entire Western community, and that Muslims felt those positive feelings and that they benefitted from them. They made the most of those feelings.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The mandate was constructed in a way that was much more supportive of the Bosnian government. Our whole presence allowed food and assistance to flow and allowed the lines to stabilise while they rearmed, yes. The whole -- the whole mandate behind UNPROFOR was more attractive to the Bosnian government than the Bosnian Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's continue with General Rose's words: [In English] "As a result, relations between the UN and the Bosnian Serbs became lastingly and immeasurably more difficult after the Bosnia army offensive. On the 20th of September at a meeting in Pale, helped it prevent the Serbs from cutting off the electricity, water and gas to Sarajevo, in response to the Bosnian attack, Karadzic subjected Viktor and me to an angry diatribe, 'How can you talk about the restoration of utilities to the Muslims in Sarajevo when they have just attacked us with heavy weapons in breach of the Airport Agreement and the NATO ultimatum? How can you raise such issues when they have systematically refused to talk about a cessation of hostilities, and the international community have subjected us to economic sanctions which are causing our people to live far worse than the citizens of Sarajevo? How dare you complain on behalf of leadership that cares so little for its own people.' "Viktor, who was generally treated with a certain deferences by the Bosnian Serbs," [No interpretation] No, that's not how it was. It is just an assumption that the Russian. [In English] "Viktor was visibly shaken by Karadzic's anger, Reiterated the fact that we had publicly condemned the action of the Bosnian government and to respond to the Bosnian attack would merely strengthen the image of a city under siege and that would not help the Serbs. Karadzic eventually calmed down and said he would reconnect the Sarajevo utilities if, in return, the Bosnian government allowed the electricity lines that passed through Bosnian territory to Banja Luka to be repaired. This seems a reasonable trade-off. A civilian subcommittee of the UN normally dealt with the restoration of utilities in Bosnia, but their negotiations had remained, until then, in a state of deadlock." [Interpretation] Do you agree that at that meeting I was angry at the beginning and that the end of the meeting was constructive and positive?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact words at the meeting, but if this is correctly quoted, then this is exactly what we -- I didn't like, which is that you were linking a military attack with the fact that you would cut off utilities, electricity and water and gas. So first of all, there was that linkage which struck some of us as inhuman, from military to the suffering of the people; and second was this statement about your people living far worse than the citizens of Sarajevo. It was completely delusional, and it was so far from reality that we can hardly emphasise it enough. So if the quotations are correct, which I assume they -- they are, they are very illustrative of precisely the problems we had at that time. With the other side, but also with yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, we will provide another document. We were not thinking of putting it forth today, but you said yourself something about how our people are living anyway. Our backs were against the wall. There were UN sanctions, sanctions by Yugoslavia, and now you will see the assessment by General Rose that life in Grbavica, which was much worse than in that other part of Sarajevo. But let's go back to this text. I don't see anywhere here, Mr. Harland, that I am going to cut off anything. We're talking about the restoration, not that I will suspend or cut it off and then let it through, and this was done after this offensive which destroyed all of those facilities. So there is some difference if I say whether I am going to allow the restoration, and of course I do have some right to some anger, at least at the beginning of the meeting because the United Nations were not protecting us but protecting our opponents; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: The water and gas and electricity lines were not cut off by the offensive. They were cut off because you cut them off. Occasionally an electricity line could be cut or something, but certainly your statement here, "How can you talk about the restoration of utilities, that is water and gas and electricity ..." it's not possible that in a one-day attack that the shooting should incidentally cut all of the water and gas and electricity lines. This was just your normal way of retaliating. They would attack militarily and you would, you know, retaliate against 2- or 300.000 civilians, and it struck us as a little barbaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let me remind you, Mr. Harland, that one single shell hit a relay or a repeater station, and that's why Bacevo did not have any electricity. Without electricity in Bacevo, Sarajevo is left without water. And if you remember correctly, every time we had a restoration then a repairman would be able to go, accompanied by UNPROFOR, to fix the installations. It was not a question of a valve or something. There had to be some infrastructure repair. Sometimes it would be just a single shell that would cause the damage, and if the electricity was cut off there would be no water. But as far as that is concerned, as far as water supplies and everything, there are orders of mine forbidding any means of that sort as a means of war waging. And you will admit, Mr. Harland, that the international community applied much worse sanctions towards the Serbs than the Serbs ever did towards the citizens of Sarajevo. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That is completely delusional. I would travel extensively throughout Republika Srpska, and the situation of the civilian population was vastly better, vastly better, Dr. Karadzic, than the situation of the civilians caught in the enclaves controlled by the Bosnian government forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Would you agree, Mr. Harland, that Banja Luka had a right to electricity, that nothing could function there without electricity, and that as General Rose says, that was a fair, a reasonable trade-off? Why would Sarajevo have -- why should Sarajevo have electricity whereas the entire Bosnian Krajina did not have electricity because they did not want to repair the electricity pylons? We were fixing everything that needed to be fixed in Sarajevo, quite a lot, but anything that Banja Luka needed was not repaired. Was that something that was fair or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, life in Banja Luka was like life in Beverly Hills compared to life in Sarajevo. This is a completely delusional line of questioning. There was simply no comparison.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Fortunately, Mr. Harland, I am just using your documents and documents of the Muslim side and this book by General Rose.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we tender this document by General Rose, the book by General Rose, this excerpt, and it's Exhibit 1D3037. The book we plan to use quite a lot in our cross-examination. And you can see this sentence: "[In English] The subcommittee of the UN normally dealt with the restoration of utilities in Bosnia, but then negotiations had remained until then in a state of deadlock." [Interpretation] Until we said, all right, but if Banja Luka gets electricity as well, there was no chance of this going through. And we had a large number of men, women, and children there. Can we tender this excerpt from the book, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Of course I have no objection, Your Honour. I'm just wondering procedurally how we might be inclined to do this, especially since Dr. Karadzic has indicated that there's going to be other excerpts from the book coming, but maybe that's best addressed next excerpt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My understanding is that if the additional part is to be admitted, that will be added to the existing number as discussed in advance between the parties. So with that understanding, we'll admit this part of his book as?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D162, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can I ask for D1403, which I need to do because of your reference -- or actually because you disputed that. You disagreed that life in Republika Srpska was worse. So can we please look at this document. This is a Muslim bulletin by the defence ministry the security administration dated the 3rd of April, 1994. This is before September, before the events in September.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not in the courtroom? I mean in e-court. 403. 1D403. If not, perhaps we can put it on the ELMO, just this one page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We should have it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we have it. Let's have the first page to identify the document, and then let us look at the last page, first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, we saw this kind of -- this format before, but are you familiar with this kind of document which is called "Bilten"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was not familiar with them during the war, but I have seen them since the war. They are publications of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Can we look at page 2 now of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Going to -- I'm going to read the part that is marked: "According to information of the military security service of the 1st Corps, the area of responsibility of the 102nd Motorised Brigade of the 2nd Battalion was toured by General Michael Rose accompanied by four officers. While touring the facilities that the fighters were using in order to prepare for departure to the front, Mr. Rose talked with the soldiers who were there and explained to them that the part of the army under the control of the army has started to live with a different life. It has started to awaken, in parentheses, and is more or is better supplied than Grbavica, which is desolate and without food." Grbavica was under Serbian control, was it not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Grbavica was under Serbian control, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So we must agree that General Rose estimated already in early April 1994 that the Serbs were living much worse than the other part of Sarajevo. This is something that we cannot dispute; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, of course we can dispute it. Grbavica is a tiny part of Sarajevo surrounded on three sides by Bosnian government held territory. But anybody in Grbavica was completely safe if they went just a few hundred metres away beyond Vraca, whereas almost 300.000 people were caught in Sarajevo with nowhere to go and were exposed to everything. And if the people of Grbavica went more than a few hundred metres away, if they went over the -- behind this cemetery on Vraca ridge, there was no shelling, no shooting. I would go there. The life was normal. You could buy a good meal. You could live a normal life. This is a completely wrong characterisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. Now I have to go back. I think this was admitted. You said in your testimony in the case against President Milosevic on the 5th of November, 2003, on page 286864. You said that: [In English] "To the extent of the UN monitors, sniper activities in Grbavica, it appeared that the Muslims were snipping more civilians than the Serbs." [Interpretation] So more people were getting killed in Grbavica and we're going to show your -- and Muslim reports which note only explosions in Grbavica for that day and nowhere else. So there were a number of days where explosions are recorded only at Grbavica and not anywhere else. So Mr. Harland, would you agree that the area behind Vraca and the entire area of Republika Srpska was subject to sanctions?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is a major difference between subject to sanctions and being subject to mortar and shell-fire every day. And I -- you keep confusing, deliberately, I think, Grbavica, which is a few hundred metres of exposed territory, which thousands and thousands of square kilometres of Republika Srpska that was completely safe and where there was plenty to eat and where food and wine and alcohol could be obtained easily and people could travel. Things are being mixed up here to give a completely false characterisation of the situation in Sarajevo and other areas, in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, it's time for me to say a no. You keep saying that, but let us now look at this document, 09632. I have to keep adding documents that I wasn't planning to so that you can see how all this looks. This is your document. You drafted it. It's actually sent by Victor Andreev to Sergio De Mello, and this is Prosecution document 09632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is also one of the associate exhibits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now that we've seen the cover page, can we now look at page 4, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At the bottom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What would you say to the previous document, 1D403?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Marked for identification pending translation, I would think, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. That will be done.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D163, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Serbian version it's page 4 as well: [In English] "BH authorities feel somewhat [indiscernible] that Sarajevo gets so much attention when their humanitarian situation which is much worse is largely ignored by the international community." [Interpretation] They are reporting from Mostar, the Muslim community, but also throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina. Muslim territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina is jealous of Sarajevo, and Republika Srpska is also without electricity under sanctions, production is halted, and I don't believe that that assessment of yours is all right, first of all. I would say it was the fact that your sensitivity toward Serbian troubles was not the same as the sensitivity towards Bosnian troubles. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we look at the next page of this document. 403. It's already been marked, but I just would like you to see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need to put away the document in English, and we need to bring back 403, please. 1D403, the previous document that we looked at. And can we look at page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read a paragraph marked with 2: "The military security service of the 2nd Corps through a source acquired information that Captain John White and Mark, military planners, spent a few days in Sarajevo recently as an advance team for a large group of American military experts who are supposed to arrive at our country. They came -- they brought a letter by -- signed by a certain Colin Lionel with them, in which he is asking General Michael Rose to provide them all the possible co-operation and help. Captain White, a member of the air force parachute units expressed particular interest in the work of our ham radio operators, how much they were working for the BH Army and how reliable their information is." Have you heard of this particular piece of information. Do you know anything about this John White, and Mark, and Colin Lionel?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 20188. I think this is a Prosecution document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, do you agree that some organisations, military organisations, from the United States were present and engaged in Bosnia and Herzegovina in providing help to them?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think the number is 21088, Prosecution Exhibit, 21088. This should be Mr. Harland's document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were aware that they were -- the Bosnian government was receiving external assistance for its military effort and that this was supported by -- by the United States in some way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In the meantime, previous document 9632 will be admitted as Prosecution exhibit?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that has been admitted as Exhibit P827 already.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, this is your document and Mr. Andreev's document of the 16th of July, 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to page 5 of the document. Page 5 of this document. Towards the bottom, Bosnian Serbs, and the penultimate paragraph. I'm going to read it in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [In English]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "Power (and hence water) and gas began to flow to Sarajevo. The sporadic nature of these supplies appeared, as before, to be caused more by the interference of the BH than by the Serbs." [Interpretation] So you yourselves were also aware of this, and you wrote it down that water depends on electricity and that these sporadic disruptions in the supply were caused more often by the Muslim army than by the Serbs or Serbian army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were aware that they also interfered with the utilities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The document says that they are more responsible, in that sense, than the Serbs; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the point of writing, yes, it must have been our assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can I have 08974, please. And was the previous document admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: As Prosecution exhibit? It's one of the associate exhibit as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As 65 ter 21088 will be P835.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 08974 now, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, I'm sorry that we're doing something that an investigative judge would be doing in our system who would then differentiate or discriminate between what is the truth and what is not. So we don't -- we would not have to go into the whole process of establishing that ourselves. Anyway, this is an order from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, which is ordering: "Pursuant to an order of the President of Republika Srpska, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, based on the current political situation and in order to resolve the problem of Sarajevo I hereby order: "Regiment and brigade commands shall immediately take the following measures. "The Ilidza Light Infantry Brigade shall ensure that water and gas are provided to the population of Sarajevo and after repairs have been carried out of the electricity installation." So we see that they were damaged. Then: "All units forbidden to fire on Sarajevo proper unless defending VRS positions." Then it goes on to say: "The unnecessary and uncontrolled firing on Sarajevo is causing great harm to the Republika Srpska. Be in full control and render impossible the unnecessary firing on Sarajevo unless it is to defend the position of the RS army. "Brigade regiment commanders are responsible for the realisation of this order." Now we're talking about the 15th of July, 1993, deputy commander of the corps, Dragomir Milosevic, at the time is ordering that my order be executed, and the order states that the water supply depends on electricity, and as soon as the electrical installations are repaired, it instructs that water should be turned on; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document seems to come from the middle of July 1993. So it's at the height of the Igman offensive, which means it's precisely one of the moments when NATO is threatening to attack. So an order by you to improve the situation with water and gas and electricity and sniping and shelling would be very consistent with what we discussed last week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, now I would have to be the one to say no. I am not asking you about our motives. I'm asking you whether this is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it's correct. It would fit that pattern.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But we will have the opportunity to discuss the Igman crisis with somebody else. We handed over the Igman zone to you, to UNPROFOR, but they entered through that zone and killed 20 of our medical workers. An entire company of medics were killed by people who had crossed over through that zone. I did not get cross about private matters, but as far as professional things and the people, that is something that I did get angry about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will admit this as RK document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P836, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it also one of the associated exhibits? I doubt it. Oh, yes. Thank you. And then --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please note in the transcript that the witness answered yes. It was of not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure there was a question, but I definitely recall the -- the act when Bosnian government forces crossed through the zone from which the Serbs had withdrawn and killed a group of medics. I -- I recall that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will have a break for 45 minutes. We'll resume at quarter to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay. One more session, Mr. Karadzic, for today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If Mr. Harland is not defensive in his defence of the UN, and I'm not attacking the UN, we will get a fair amount of work done today, I hope. This is a document that we've admitted, right, this order issued by General Milosevic. It has been assigned a number, Excellency, hasn't it? Can I now have D123. Sorry, 321.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: 321, Mr. Harland. I will do my best to use as few Serb documents as possible, so I hope that there will be as few "Nos" as possible and as many "Yeses" as possible. So this is the bulletin of the 25th of April, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have page 3 now, please. Of this document, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that General Divjak said that about 75 per cent of the Muslim army waged war in their own civilian clothes? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it sound familiar, though, that they waged war mostly wearing their own clothes?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time I arrived, most of them had uniforms. Actually, I think they were uniforms from the former East Germany, but by the time I arrived they almost all had camouflage, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, this is the end of April, so it's a bit before your time. The third page, starting with "According." This is their report. The security administration is providing information to the Main Staff: "According to the assessment of the commander of the 101st Motorised Brigade of the 1st Corps, the combat morale in his unit has slowly started to decline. There are many reasons for this situation, various rumours and negative propaganda included. There are some rumours in the units of this brigade to the effect that the president of the Presidency received from an Arab president 10.000 US dollars for cigarettes for the army, but they did not receive. Also they should buy 120.000 uniforms, but they did not do that, instead the soldiers are still fighting in their own jeans and sneakers. Besides that, they transferred to the town drinks, cigarettes, oranges, bananas and other goods which were exclusively used for smuggling instead of providing weapons and ammunition. Also in the city there are opened cafe and other private shops and their owners are very often members of the army who resell stolen goods -- who have been reselling stolen goods from the beginning of the war, et cetera. Also many -- there are a lot of negative comments concerning the division. Then there is Cele and Caco and other criminals. Does this sound convincing? This is their very own report.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can it be admitted, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, you must have said yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I note that the translation that we have isn't a translation of the whole document, so I would still be prepared to agree to MFI pending translation of the whole document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long is the original? I haven't checked.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's a four-page document, and we have around two pages of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: One page of translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D164, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is possible that this may be the next document. Let's have a look. No. Do you know Stefan Lot, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to this document, it is 046 -- the ERN number is 0465537. That's the ERN number. The previous document can be removed if it's been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: For the record, I note that Mr. Harland answered no to the question whether he knew Mr. Stefan Lot.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I have 1D479, please, special information, the 21st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were there by then, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we don't have a translation, but I'm going to read out the important parts. This is special information provided by the security administration to the Main Staff of the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I please have page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Some information and data received from Stefan Lot, liaison officer of UNPROFOR attached to the command of the 1st Corps before he left that duty. And then towards the middle of the first paragraph it says: "In relation to the situation in town, Lot said that no one in UNPROFOR understands that in this kind of war situation there are many people in the streets, that cafes are open as well as some privately owned shops. Also, many people go to work. However, not a single company is working." This assessment is a bit different from yours, that in Grbavica and Republika Srpska it is fine, whereas it is bad out there. Don't you agree that this is somewhat different?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't really understand what he said, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he says that everyone in UNPROFOR is surprised at this relaxed atmosphere, that everybody's out in the streets, cafes and restaurants are open, everybody's milling about but nobody works. No companies are working and everybody lives well. That's what he is saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did he really say everybody lives well? No, surely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, he says that cafes are open and privately owned shops, and these cafes and shops cannot be working if there's no one buying in those shops.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some cafes open, and there were shops, and there were the markets, but they had the most miserable produce. And it's true that people would come out. They would go mad just sitting inside, but there was nothing much to -- to buy, and it was extremely dangerous. And whoever this colleague of mine, Mr. Lot is, I'm sure he cannot have been saying that there was anything like normal life going on within the besieged area of Sarajevo. It was -- it was a horror. I mean, some kids managed to go to school, but for most it was just awful. But it's true that there were some cafes open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let us now have a look at another paragraph. His assessment is that, "it is inevitable that our side will lose the war if things go on this way." He also said that everyone in UNPROFOR is aware of the problems in relation to different military police units, Celo, Caco, and similar commanders outside the city of Sarajevo who do not obey orders issued by superior commands, pointing out that for this kind of disobedience heads would role in the French Army. Members of UNPROFOR have the impression that political structures are obstructing the defence system and that it is only the BH Army that is defending the state, and relations between political structures in the army seem unclear to them. He also says that a serious problem for the BH Army are the disagreements with the Sandzak line, and he does not understand -- can we have the next page. In the next, he says that Sefer Halilovic is a greedy man who is a toy in the hands of politicians, and so on and so forth. Do you know that the families of many of the top Muslim people lived in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, sorry. No, I didn't -- I didn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
