utterances.text: On this second page, towards the bottom, it also says that he said that: "UNPROFOR has information about our ammunition production as well as of hand grenades and rifle grenades in town, and that they know exactly in which buildings this production is taking place." He also knows that oil is purchased in the black market from UNPROFOR members, but that will be brought to an end because in Sarajevo soon it will only be the French soldiers who will be there. Obviously he believes in the French Army, Stefan Lot, and obviously there were these national differences in respect of your views regarding the conflicts; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Valentin Tomasev [phoen] is?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, Colonel Valentin, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: At one point this report says that Stefan Lot said that Valentin has a high regard for Hajrulahovic as a true professional, and he got the impression that Valentin wanted to advise Hajrulahovic in some actions. Well, we have been traditionally friends with the French, and I would be sorry if he advised Hajrulahovic in terms of his actions against us. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that a lot of my colleagues, including General Rose whose opinions you've just seen, also had a rather high opinion of Mustafa Hajrulahovic as a professional soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he ever help him with advice, I mean UNPROFOR officers?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so, but he would often visit General Rose when I was there, but I think it was it was a cordial professional relationship. I think General Rose was of the view that militarily the Bosnian army was extremely weak, badly equipped, badly led, bad tactical positions, and he was generally happy to meet somebody he considered a professional and talented soldier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please. There is no translation, I think.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can it be marked for identification?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With that proviso, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, that will be MFI D165.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's mark pending translation, I make it clear. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. 1D458, please. Could I have that now? I'm afraid that we don't have a translation of that document either. 1D458. Or actually, perhaps we do. Yes, we do. It's the 6th of June. Now that we've identified the first page, could we please have the second page, "Destructive activity by Musan Topalovic, Caco." That is the heading. We'll see that document as well, but we are actually asking for 1D458. It should be the right number. 14 -- or 1D458. 458, that's the number we have, and that should be right, but here we see another document. We'll be needing that document pretty soon, too, but ... All right. Let's -- no. No. Can we have this placed on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But which is what, Mr. Karadzic? I checked the number, and the document we are seeing through the monitor is 1D458, unless there's a mistake in numbering.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that there must have been a mistake. Of course, we'll be dealing with this document soon as well, but sorry -- ah, yes, that's it. Yes, yes. That's it. This is right. Now let us have page number 2, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Then we'll just deal with this document now. Actually, can the other one be placed on the ELMO, because we won't get our order right if we don't do it that way. So can we please place this on the overhead projector. There has been a change. 04035 and -- the page numbers are right here in what I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Do we have any idea of what the 65 ter number of this is document might be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No translation at all. So if you could tell us what document it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a special information provided by the intelligence service of the Muslim army. The pages are 03570398, 78, and now it is 04035980, 81 and 82.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Without any cover page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I understand things, it is part of this special information, and it has its number, 04035982. The cover page says "Special information," 04035979. And then the next one is 980.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's see how we can get on with -- put your question.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You did know something about what was going -- about what was going on in Sarajevo, what happened to civilians and how they were being treated by these commanders, especially of the 109th and 110th Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Now, the last paragraph on the second page. The cover page and then the first page and then the second page. I'm going to read it carefully. Fikret Muslimovic is reporting. He is the chief of military security and he is reporting to his command. He says: "We note that as regards the unlawful and destructive activity of Musan Topalovic, Caco, we have provided information several times already, and in this connection we have proposed certain measures in order to make it impossible for him to behave that way. Inter alia, in a document that we sent on the 1st of December, 1992, when the 10th Mountain Brigade was still in the process of being established and Caco as one of the candidates for its commander, we presented the information we had available on his mistreatment and arrest of citizens and even his own soldiers. Liquidations of citizens who were ethnic Serbs. Forced mobilisation and taking citizens to dig trenches. Among these citizens there were sick people and disabled people. Also, apartments were broken into, humanitarian aid was being looted, and so on." So that was written in June 1993, and in December 1994, all the authorities knew what Musan Topalovic, Caco, was doing in town, that he was arresting people randomly in the street. He was slaughtering Serbs, literally slaughtering them. You will see that from the documents that are to come now. And how is it that no one from the international community stepped in to protect these miserable people in Sarajevo who were being treated that way?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, if the English translation of your remarks was right, there was a reference to December of 1994, but he was long dead by December 1994. He was killed by the Bosnian government for just these types of activities in, I think, October of 1993. I must say I -- I have never met Mr. Muslimovic, I don't think, but I have a generally positive impression. If this is an internal report of a Bosnian army saying that a Bosnian army commander has been abusing or has liquidated people because of their Serb nationality, and on the basis of this, that the Bosnian army then got rid of him and when he resisted he was killed, I would say it is indicative of the fact that there was a major problem with gangsterism and criminality. But it's last major sign of seriousness that they were addressing it, and they had even identified as one of his crimes the fact that he was committing crimes against people of Serb nationality. So I don't see -- he was a well-known criminal. In the documents we've looked at which I've signed, there's also references to his actions. So I have nothing against this report here by Mr. Muslimovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can see from the previous document that UNPROFOR knew about it and Stefan Lot knew and inquired about this, but -- but Mr. Harland, this is not anyone. This is a brigade commander whom the government and the authorities were tolerating for a whole year until he slaughtered all these Serbs. He moved into Serbian apartments, and then they killed him. And do you know after why they did that? That was after he killed the son of the minister of the interior, Avdo Hebib, and organised an armed uprising. And then documents that we will show will indicate that he was not killed because of the Serbs but because of the fact that he started to get in the way and started kill them; is that correct? Do you know that the son of the minister of the interior, Avdo Hebib, was killed, and that the son was killed by Caco?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I -- you were correcting me on the sequence of events, but I was there when that -- when those events to place, and if I remember correctly, the Bosnian government and UNPROFOR had become extremely alarmed by the behaviour of this man. Now, you are right in saying that he committed crimes against citizens of Serb nationality on the basis of their nationality, but he also committed crimes against the population at large, and his -- the little part of Sarajevo that was under his control, I think near the brewery, yeah, was more or less a no-go zone for everybody. And I think the sequence was that the Bosnian government tried to arrest him; then he grabbed the people; then he killed the son of Avdo Hebib, the minister of the interior; then he was killed. So my understanding of this was: He was an out-of-control commander, in what was a very chaotic defence of Sarajevo, and the document you've presented is illustrative of an effort by the Bosnian government to gain some -- restore some sort of order and decency in the -- in the military establishment, which was successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The Bosnian government would kiss you for these explanations, but it wasn't like that, but you are correct, this was December 1992, not December 1994. But if we accept this document, I would ask for 1D453, and then you will see that it is not the way it was presented to you. I don't believe that you wanted it to be like that yourself, but it was presented to you like that. The document is 1D453. It wasn't translated. The date is the 7th and the 8th of May, 1993, about the state of security on the -- or the security situation on the 7th and 8th of May, 1993. And then in the penultimate paragraph it says -- this is a brigade, Mountain Brigade. This is Caco's brigade that we're talking about. It says: "In any case, the security organs had the exceptional honour today, as well as the very complex task of executing all security actions in a very professional manner in order that the visit by Mr. Izetbegovic, the President of the Presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to our brigade would proceed in the best possible way. "At the time of the writing of this report, 14.45 hours, the president is still our guest and we hope that the visit will be completed successfully in every way." So six months after being informed about the fact that Musan Topalovic, Caco, was expending the Serbs around him and was throwing him into Kazani -- we will explain that later. Have you heard of Kazani?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Alija Izetbegovic is visiting. And this isn't the only time that he is visiting this brigade. So he's visiting this brigade and you can see that nevertheless, the 10th Mountain Brigade was not a renegade unit but was, so to say, under the protection of Alija Izetbegovic. And we're talking about May 1993 here; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't say that. Would I say that the defence of Sarajevo was an extremely diverse coalition of people. There were nationalists, there were Islamists, there were criminals, there were psychopaths, there were good citizens, there were democrats, and there were a lot of people who were simply confused to be the object of attack from Serb forces, and they had nothing in common except they were all under attack by you. And I think what brought them together, this very strange group of people, this strange collection of people, was the common horror that was inflicted upon them. And what the documents you have been showing in fact show the process that the government was going through of weeding out some of the more psychopathic and criminal elements. I would not say that all the psychopathic and criminal elements were eliminated, and you are right that the president and others attempted to make compromises with some of them. But this document that you have showed from this man is an extremely interesting historical document, as it shows that process of trying to make a state out of what was a very strange collection of people being attacked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then we will use more time, more time than I planned. Are you trying to say that Mr. Izetbegovic went to visit Caco, gave him this death sower, this machine-gun 84, and went to lecture him not to slit the throats of Serbs any more? Is this something that you would do with a seasoned criminal about whom he had known for at least six months that he had killed Serbs from the Old Town and threw them into Kazani? I cannot agree with that even though you did explain very well this composition of the force that was defending Sarajevo. I wouldn't explain that better myself. Does this document indicate that Izetbegovic was visiting the brigade that Caco was commander of? Is that so or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: That appears to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm a bit concerned about the number of documents that have been -- that haven't been translated. It's difficult for us to follow. The same is true, no doubt, with the witness. So bear that in mind in presenting the document to the witness. So we deal with two documents, the previous document which was put on ELMO and as well as this one, 1D453. Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I have no objection to their admission. I'd just like to note, in the first document that appeared on the ELMO was shown to me for the first time when my friend brought a copy to me. It was not on any list of released documents that we were able to identify, and in fact, that's the only point I'd like to make, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It seems to have some ERN number or -- of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It does indeed, Your Honour, which is why I was limiting my point, but it would still be useful to have notification of these things ahead of time to be able to, at least, read the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. While we mark them for identification, Mr. Karadzic, you are advised to tell the Prosecution as to the provenance of that document, the previous one. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document that was placed on the ELMO will be MFI D166, and 1D453 will be MFI D167.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both documents, Your Excellencies, are from the EDS. As for the translation, believe me, my family, my relatives have been translating. They're all scattered from Pale to Canada. We cannot keep up. These documents were sent for translation almost three months ago. So where I come from, if somebody's not able to complete something within a dead-line, within three months, then they would close shop. So if we cannot keep up with the translations, well, then we need to see what we can do. I would now like us to look at 1D510. Joking aside, but I really believe that we would need to have more resources available, because I cannot really keep up any more. I am giving my friends and relatives translations, and they're doing them for free. Anyway, let's look at 1D510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't like to waste time for being involved in this kind of discussion, but my understanding is that you are receiving remuneration for your assistant, which should include translation as well. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excellency, I did comment while we were waiting for the documents. As for the remuneration, you know what that is. This is pursuant to your decisions to my motions appealing. Anyway, this is from the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, security administration. On the 2nd of January, 1993, they interviewed Nihad Hodzic, who was a member of the 10th Mountain Brigade, and it says at the bottom of the page that he was wounded in Mrkovici, and Mrkovici is a Serb village where he should not have gone in the first place. And now we can look for page 5. Page 5 of this document. This is a Muslim document. In this interview, he says -- I don't know if we have that on page 4. Page 5. Page 5 in the English as well: "About the alleged --" "I don't know anything about the alleged visits made by the officers of the SVK, but I did hear that Alija Izetbegovic once visited the 10th Mountain Brigade before I was wounded and gave us a sower of death. One night, I do not recall the exact date, but I think that it was in mid-October 1993. I came to the brigade command. I came across the commander Musan Topalovic, Caco, in front of the brigade with a military vehicle. He stopped and told me to sit with him in the PUH vehicle, in the back where a couple of young men of a certain age. Their heads were bent forward. They were wearing civilian clothes," and then there is a sentence below that: "We stopped there and continued on foot towards Kazani. On the way there, towards the front lines, we were joined by one of the snipers whose nickname was Cuto. He took one of those young men and Caco took the other one, and they took them forward. We were also joined by the snipers' commander Omer Tendzo and the sniper Asif." And then below that, it says: "Caco took the smaller man, shoved him to the ground and kicked him two to three times in the head. At that time, I was standing off to the side, and the other man, young man, was sitting on the ground. Caco then called me and told me, 'Come on. Do you want to kill him?'" And then a little bit lower: "Caco was holding a large knife in his hands. He came up to me and gave me the knife and then says, 'Come on, slit his throat.' I was still standing like that for some time. Then Caco told me, 'Come on, don't make me slit your throat or to bring your wife and kids here and slit their throats.'" And then a few lines below that: "Then I approached him from the right, bent over him and then crossed my knife two or three times over the throat of the young man. Blood gushed out of his throat. The man did not show any signs of resistance. "After slashing my knife against his throat, I left the knife, turned around and moved away. I started towards the bunker nearby and turned around and saw Caco continuing to slash the head of the same man." And then a little bit lower down: "They brought the second man to that spot and Caco started kicking him. Then I saw him starting to stab him across his body. I did not hear the man scream or anything to that effect. In the meantime, there was another young man who appeared, who was tall, 180 metres," and so on. This is something that a Muslim fighter from the 10th Brigade stated, 10th Mountain Brigade, describing the actions of his commander Caco Topalovic in slitting the throats of two Serb young men who were not even defending themselves. They were resigned to their fate. What do you say to this?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think we -- I said before that he was a psychopath and that I was interested in the document from Mr. Muslimovic because it showed a serious attempt to identify that even when that psychopathic behaviour was demonstrating itself against Serb victims that the Bosnian government did slowly sort itself out and gets rid of him. Yeah, he was a monster, and this crime at Kazani, which, of course, is extremely widely known and reported is an example of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, we'll have further 40 minutes today, and by -- by the end of today's session I think you will have had about nine hours and a half. How much longer do you have for this cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I hope that we will have those four and a half hours tomorrow. It will be good to have those full 14 hours if Mr. Harland is unable to come at any time. He is a very valuable witness, except for this understanding for the Bosnian government, everything else, all the facts are valuable and there's nobody who could explain to us things as they were, just facts without any explanations. And if we will not have this full amount of time, then I would kindly ask for Mr. Harland to be recalled and to complete his testimony another time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before coming to the courtroom today I was advised by VWS that Mr. Harland has to leave the Tribunal tomorrow by 1.00 to catch the flight to Haiti. So I inquired around whether we can start at 8.30 tomorrow morning to save time, if any. So I thank everybody for their generous understanding in terms of security, interpreters, and court reporters. So we will start at 8.30 tomorrow morning, but we have to leave at -- you have to leave at least an hour for the redirect. So bear that in mind and concentrate on relevant questions in order not to omit any important questions. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can I tender this document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D168.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1D338, please, just briefly, because I would like to substantiate this particular matter. 1D338, please. I believe that we also have the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is also a security administration document. The date is the 6th of November, 1993. I think I saw a translation earlier. Perhaps we don't have one. This is Haskic, Enes, nickname Zela, who stated: "On the 2nd of July, 1993, at about 2100 hours, I was sitting at the command of the 10th Mountain Brigade when Musan Topalovic, Caco, called and asked that I bring 20 to 50 fighters to the command of the 10th Brigade Bistrik." And it goes on to say, this is now on page 3 of this document, that President Alija Izetbegovic went to see Caco twice and allegedly gave him some foreign currency, funds for the needs of his brigade. The Reis-Ulema Ceric also came as well as Sefer Halilovic. General Briquemont from UNPROFOR also came to see Caco at one time, and so on and so forth. This was an important figure in the Muslim military, and you can see that Mr. Izetbegovic had no intention of preventing him from doing anything. He gave him foreign currency funds. He gave him a machine-gun, and he was somebody who a welcomed visitor there. Does all of that arise from this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm hesitating because I'm not sure that General Briquemont went to see Caco. One could ask General Briquemont that fact, but we had extreme limitations we put on ourselves about seeing Caco because he was such a psychopathic person. But in general, I would say that there is no doubt that President Izetbegovic did want to -- did work with people who he thought could contribute to the defence of the city even when they were people who were clearly extremely undesirable, at least up to a point. So the general contention that he met with him and may have had a positive interaction with him I would not doubt, but I have a little doubt about what it says about General Briquemont there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I can confirm that General Briquemont is one of the most exceptional figures that we had, and if he really did go there, then it was probably an attempt to set something right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: Your indulgence for just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting can we look at 1D478.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: I actually want to rise on the relevance of this document, Your Honour, because the question to my -- to Mr. Harland was in regard to General Briquemont, and he answered the question as regards General Briquemont and General Briquemont's character. That being the case, I turn to the remainder of the document, which has -- other than for that one sentence with respect to General Briquemont, has absolutely no bearing on the question of General Briquemont but is full of what might appear to be the beginnings of some tu quoque issues, a litany of alleged crimes against Serbs. So I would object, Your Honour, on the grounds of relevance of this document.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the decision -- if I may say something.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can say something before your decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So while we are deliberating, we can't hear anything, so -- but we find it generally relevant to -- relevant to the general situation, so as such we will admit it while marking it for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D169.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, did you want to say anything?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've said it all, Your Excellencies, and this is introduction to the further development of things where Muslims are being killed and Sefer Halilovic's wife and her -- and her brother are killed, and this is something that is ascribed to the Serbs, but it was discovered that it was not a Serbian shell but explosives. So this is very relevant. Can we look at 1D468. 478.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting, I would just like to remind Mr. Harland that at that time internal struggles were going on in Sarajevo, and Sefer Halilovic happened to a victim of that. His wife and her brother were killed in an explosion, and before then we see how their conversations with tapped. This is a document signed by Enver Mujezinovic on the 12th of July, 1993. Now, I would like to look at page 2. On page 2, it says: "Operational and technical measures and operational activities are undertaken to clarify the motives and goals of armed rebellion of a number of the 9th Motorised Brigade members as well as the 10th Mountain Brigade, as well as special unit Delta which happened in the night between the 2nd and 3rd of July of this year in the municipality of Stari Grad. Some information displayed the positions and creation of the subject Hasa." That's Sefer Halilovic. He kept a very low profile during all these events. We see that this was an armed rebellion of the 9th Motorised and the 10th Mountain Brigade, Mr. Harland, don't we?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, apparently. I haven't even this document before, but yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So he was killed after that. He wasn't killed because he had slaughtered Serbs. And now let's go to page 4 in the same document. Page 4. Where it says: Hasa or Sefer Halilovic talked to Delic, and Delic asked him whether he had sent somebody to pacify Delta who were under control of Delic. He said Mido, standing for Midhat Aljic, the personal escort of Sefer Halilovic, said that it would be dangerous to go anywhere because there is shooting going on at several places. At the bottom of this page Dzevad Radjo wanted to know whether Hasa undertook measures to release those who had been forcefully taken away to dig trenches. Hasa answered I can't do anything tonight. So this is not only about the rebellion of one unit. It is obvious that some high-ranking officers were also suspects and that there was the reason for their inner struggle rather than any Serb victims. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I would agree that clearly the fact that he's been victimising Serbs is not the only thing that the Bosnian government had against him, and it was probably not enough for them to move against him. But, in fact, this transcript, like the earlier document from Mr. Muslimovic, does seem to confirm that they were at least making a serious internal effort to put their house in order. This -- it says in the English transcription, "Believe me, Fikret acted there very amateurishly. He had enough material to arrest him five months before that." You see this clearly what we're looking at is a document which shows how they are attempting to take some appropriate action, and they are aware that it's too late and they need to establish some order. So I -- I agree with you that the crimes against Serbs were not sufficient to make the government move against him, but they were trying to establish some sort of lawful state there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now look at page 9 in this same document. It says here in repeated conversation Hasa put pressure on Muslimovic to release those criminals that had been arrested and he said, Think maybe it would be good. I'm not insisting. However when the investigates is completed, maybe you should say, Lads, go home. And criminal reports should still be filed. When the meeting was over, when the goals of the meeting were achieved, we will then tear up the criminal reports, and that's a conversation between Muslimovic and Hasa on the 23rd of June -- June, 1993. I wouldn't go on elaborating and analysing this document. You can see that this is just playing games, pretending that the rule of law is in place, and you will see how Muslimovic implores but doesn't arrest. Do you agree that it would be inadmissible in a state with the rule of law for somebody to implore with criminals not to continue their activities, and instead of that, instead of imploring them, they should be arrested and prosecuted? What do you say?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: By the time I arrived in Sarajevo, these original gangs who had -- many of them criminal gangs, some of them police, some of those who had defended Sarajevo, had a lot of power, and the government was trying to regularise the situation, to eliminate some of them, to integrate some of the others of them fully into the state structures. But the reality was they had to work with the people who had the guns and knew how to use them. So all of these documents from the one signed by Mr. Muslimovic to this one are all, in fact, very interesting historical documents which I haven't seen, basically illustrating that that process of solely establishing order. And if we then forward this just a couple of months to October, it ends with the final death of Caco and the integration of his unit into the regular structure of the -- of the 1st Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, if the other sides in Bosnia shared your understanding for the impotent [Realtime transcript read in error "impetus"] of the state, but let me remind you, Mr. Harland, the Serbs fled the cities and created their state in the fields, a green-field state without any institutions or any such thing. The Muslims, however, inherited the entire infrastructure. How is it possible then that they tolerated Caco for two years while he was killing the Serbs and only when he turned against them they started dealing with him? Is your understanding for the impotent of the Muslim government a bit too much and would you be inclined to show the same understanding for the governments of the other two peoples in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the transcript is -- is getting it's not impetus it's impotence, that's the lack of power, right, twice. Second, to answer the question, I think that the Bosnian government was almost not a government at all. It was an absolutely chaotic assembly of people who were under attack from the moment the country came -- was born and recognised, from the most criminal, to the most democratic, to the Islamists and Jihadi, all of them, and they had no physical contact with each other. When I arrived they used to have to ask us what was happening in Bihac or Mostar. They were physically separated. They had nothing in common with each other. They were under fire. They couldn't move. Whereas when you went to Republika Srpska where they were at least able to move around and communicate, they had created a functioning Assembly and army and system. So our impression was that the Bosnian government was barely a government at all, and all the documents you've shown is the process by which they were attempting to form into some coherent state structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please see the last page of that same document. I'm interested in just one sentence there and then I will be asking for 519. Before that, the last page. We have the Serbian. We need English as well. All of that information indicates that Hasa still wants to remain the number-one man in the BH Army, which is confirmed by his conversation with Senad Masovic, and so on and so forth. We're talking about a power struggle, not the struggle for a state with the rule of raw. Does this look to you like a power struggle? And nobody every mentions Serbian victims. Wouldn't you agree with me that there's no reference anywhere here to any Serb victim? It's all about a power struggle.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I mean you've shown two of these documents which do show Muslims expressing concern about Serb victims, which I consider very -- very positive, and given the fact that if one ever travelled to the Serb side of the line, precisely this was happening on a vastly greater scale and people were not removed. I consider this essentially a positive process, because when Caco was removed, the -- the crime such as the killing of those Serbs who were dumped in the Kazani pit above Bistrik, that stopped. So I think, yes, there is a power struggle, but it's a power struggle between some people who are definitely criminal and definitely -- I mean, I don't want to use a technical term in your area, but some apparently psychopathic against people who have some notion of a regularly functioning states in which those crimes would not be committed, but yes, it's a power struggle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is clear that Hasa or Sefer Halilovic -- because it says here that he still wants to be the number-one man in the army, so he's -- Sefer Halilovic. Thank you. You said there were such cases in Republika Srpska as well. We are going to prove that is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this document be admitted, please. The answer was not recorded, the witness's confirmation that Hasa is Sefer Halilovic. That was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, although the Chamber found that the previous document to be relevant despite the objection from the Defence, I'm wondering where you are leading us to. As you noted, this witness is a very important witness. Let's not dwell on -- too much on Caco or the historical background. Let's move on to your real issues. Ms. Edgerton, I take it you want the full translation of this document or are you happy with it as is?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: No, I'd like the full translation, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then that will be marked for identification pending full translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As MFI D170, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would kindly ask Mr. Harland to repeat that Hasa is Sefer Halilovic for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I haven't said anything about the authenticity of this document because I can't possibly know, but it -- it does seem consistent with what we -- with what we know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. The document confirms it. Let's -- let me explain for the participants in these proceedings. Let me say why I've taken this option. According to our information, this is a rule and not an exception. It was not just Musan Topalovic, Caco, but other commanders, save for Hajrulahovic who everybody respected. Juka Prazina became general. He had his own unit and he had special police within that unit; am I right, Mr. Harland?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ramiz Delalic, Celo, who killed a participant in the wedding party, he bragged about that on TV, was he also a criminal who had his unit in the territory of -- of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Ismet Bajramovic, Celo, was also a criminal. He was a drug addict. He was also a commander. I don't know whether he died or whether he killed himself. I believe that he committed suicide after the war. But throughout the war he was a very important military figure. He decided on the lifes -- on the life and death of the citizens. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think from the beginning of this line of questioning, Dr. Karadzic, I have agreed that the Bosnian government used anybody who was capable of fighting to defend the city, and many of those people were extremely unattractive. Some of them they got rid of, some they co-opted, and some of them they successfully integrated to the army, but it was a very -- a very diverse coalition of people, including definite criminal elements, yes, and including this last one you mention.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the court please produce 1D519 just to see what the relationship was between Alija Izetbegovic and Sefer Halilovic. Sefer Halilovic was the head of that rebellion, and when they were killed, he remained, and his wife and her brother were killed by an explosion on the terrace and not in Serb shelling. The document is 1D519, and you can see here that on the 26th of April, 1994, a decision was made by the Presidency and a decision was signed by Alija Izetbegovic about the promotion, Sefer Halilovic into a general of BiH Army. He was removed from his position, and he was replaced by General Delic as commander, but he was promoted into the rank of general. Unfortunately, the document is not on e-court by mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't think it was notified to the Prosecution as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: But if I can assist at all, document 159 was, and perhaps if Dr. Karadzic has a look at that, that might be the item he's looking for, just in case, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But, Mr. Karadzic, you are not obliged to answer, but how is this relevance to your case?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I just said that those were not incidents. That was the system, and Mr. Harland very kindly described the host of fighters who did not have to defend themselves. They were waiting for a political solution. That was a system in which there was no place for us. Those were the highest ranking officials of the state who were in cahoots with the biggest criminals, and the Serbs lost lives. They were slaughtered. They were decapitated, men, women, and children. And that was a system that existed, and I have to prove who was on the other side of the front line. It is very relevant for these proceedings. According to me, it is of the utmost importance. And by the way, many of those victims were portrayed as Serb victims, but you will see what was actually going on there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is rarely intervening with your line of questioning, but one may ask you whether your defence is that you allegedly attacked, took over, seized because of this situation. You're not obliged to answer, although I think you are already aware of the tu quoque. So I would recommend you to concentrate on the real issues. We have ten minutes. Let's get on with the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I will explain in two sentences. Media and the partiality of the Western community, the partiality of the united -- the United States of America have contribute to the picture where 1.000 shells that fell on Sarajevo were counted as hundred thousand of shells, and they were Serbs like in Dresden. And in Sarajevo, there was not a single building that was destroyed by Serb shelling. A picture was painted that the citizens of Sarajevo were just like tame pigeons being attacked by wild Serbs, and the situation was just the other way round. We were the ones who were waiting for a political solution, and there was an all-out campaign of slaughtering and killing waged against us. And all that was supported by the subjectivity of the international community which is being confirmed here and such reports about the crimes, about the crimes that the Serbs allegedly committed went on the CNN. But if Serbs were attacked, if Serbs were victims, that was never reported. There is nothing about that, not even in secret reports of the United Nations. I have to show who was on the one side of the front line and who was on the other. This is not tu quoque. We have to show what we did. We are being charged with launching attacks on a peaceful city. However, Sarajevo was a fortress which was run by criminals, and they could go on killing Serbs without being taken to charge and that was a whole system. There was not just one single criminal in the Old City of Sarajevo. There were a host of them and they were part of a system. We are charged with being in a joint criminal enterprise, and those who wanted to place the entire Bosnia under their control are not charged with anything, and the condition for that was to first expel Serbs and then Croats. Like I showed in my opening statement, and I will show by means of documents, there was a plan to expel first Serbs and then Croats from Bosnia. The Croats are the ones who discovered that before the eyes of America. We have to show that it was impossible to defend ourselves before we could prove who we are dealing with, and we were dealing with the unprecedented atrocities committed by Muslims whom we considered our own people. This is a new mentality, the mentality of the jihad, and once that settles there's no way you can restore life back to normal, and this is what we are going to prove because we have to prove it. May I go on?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Harland, did you every hear of the so-called Seve?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was a secret unit, a unit of the secret police. There was a wide coverage about the existence of that unit alleged set up by Alija Delimustafic. You will remember Herenda and you will remember Ugljen, I'm sure. And all of a sudden documents about those things went missing from Bosnia. We requested those documents, but let me tell you what Sefer Halilovic says about the alleged Serb bomb that killed his wife. The place of impact of the so-called shell, and in brackets it says in the apartment of Sefer Halilovic when Halilovic's wife and his -- her brother were killed, close bracket, is the best proof that it was not an artillery shell but that it was an imitation of an artillery shell. A MUP commission that drafted the report consisted of unskilled men who were not professionals. I know that pressure was put on some of them at the time in order to compile false reports. I'm going to report those people, because they covered up crimes. If that had not been the killing of a person affiliated to such a high-ranking military official who knew something about explosives and shells, that shell, that explosive would have been ascribed to the Serb side; right? Maybe I can assist you by reading what he says next. Would an artillery officer could have concluded with just a naked eye could also be concluded by Vehbija Karic, and that is that the effect of artillery shell would have been much more destructive than the effects caused by the explosive that exploded on the terrace, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are you putting your question? What was your question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I just wanted to present this to Mr. Harland. I wanted to tell him how all that transpired and how it was qualified by General Halilovic, and then my question will follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It is tragic -- tragic -- tragical that three shells fell at the brickworks area. As Karic says, one fell over, one fell short and the third hit the target. Several thousand of people who reside in the territory of the brickworks can testify to the fact that there was just one explosion on that day, and that was on the terrace, and that was no other shells falling on the brickworks. My question, Mr. Harland, is this: If the incident had not happened in the apartment of a general who knows about explosives and shells, do you think that that incident would have also be described to the Serbs, it would be -- it would have been reported that three shells had fallen and one of them hit the -- Halilovic's apartment? According to what you know and from your experience, do you think that that would also have been ascribed to us?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with this specific incident, but certainly from our mortar-detecting radar, the vast majority of shells, the way over 99 per cent of the shells that landed in Sarajevo, came from Serb-held positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you will see tomorrow that it wasn't like that pursuant to the expenditure of ammunition according to their reports. We have an interview here by Mr. Halilovic given to the Sarajevo Sivet [phoen] in 1998, and if we can accept this, then I have one last question from 1D474, where the report, official report, states that this woman was killed from a shell which was assumed to have been a Serb grenade -- shell. I'm not talking about the number of shells from one side or the other. What I'm talking about is that they were caught in something that was ascribed to the Serbs and that this would have slipped through had it not been Sefer Halilovic who was involved, and I just have one more thing. Perhaps we could tender that and then we will be finished for today. On the 7th of July, 1993, in the afternoon, one shell directly hit the apartment of the Chief of the Main Staff, a commander in the Ciglane neighbourhood, and on that occasion his wife and killed and her brother. In connection with this event, misinformation is already spreading according to which the case is being linked with the situation in town following the conflicts caused by the members of the 9th and the 10th Mountain Brigades. Mr. Harland, do you think that this is a correct report that Halilovic is disputing?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That it's correct in the sense that Halilovic is correct or that the police is correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVID HARLAND [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's -- I meant it's possible that there is a -- there are -- there would be grounds for him to dispute it. I don't know the context, so I can't tell you anything definite about this event. I know the organisation, though, and I worked with it in Sarajevo, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we admit these two documents, please. Would I like to move them to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Was the document that appeared before us the document you wanted to tender, i.e., 1D159?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's the interview 15 -- 59. It's very instructive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Edgerton.

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: With respect to that document, Your Honour, I would raise the same objection as I did initially.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Which is?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: It's irrelevant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And the 474?

utterances.speaker: MS. EDGERTON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 474 will be marked for identification pending translation.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be MFI D171.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will give our ruling as to the admission of 1D159 tomorrow morning when we will give our ruling as to the --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can say that the relevance also has to do with the pattern, the pattern of incidents that were ascribed to the Serbs. They would do something, and then they would say that it was a Serb shell. I think that this is something that is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will resume at half past 8.00 tomorrow morning, and I recommend you to prune your questions so as to conclude by 12.00 tomorrow. We'll rise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 11th day of May, 2010, at 8.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 5.20 p.m.
